title: “Beers Criteria” Explained: Medications Older Adults Should Avoid (or Use With Caution)
location: All Episodes: Dr Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH – Better Health While Aging
channelDescription:
If you're over 60 and want to stay sharp, active, and independent as you age, you’re in the right place. On this channel, geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH, breaks down complex health topics into clear, practical steps you can take based on the best of geriatrics and aging science.

From understanding medications and memory changes to improving nutrition and preventing falls, every video helps you age with clarity and confidence. To get weekly tips directly from Dr. K, sign up for her free newsletter below.

Supporting an aging parent or relative? Check out Dr. K’s companion channel, Helping Older Parents, where she shares videos specifically about caregiving and eldercare.

text:
Many medications help us feel better and manage chronic conditions — but as we age, medications often become riskier, especially when you’re taking several at once (polypharmacy). In fact, older adults are more likely to experience side effects, drug-drug interactions, and medication-related harm.

In this episode of the Better Health While Aging video podcast, geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH explains one of the most important medication safety tools in geriatrics: the American Geriatrics Society (AGS) Beers Criteria® — often called the “Beers List.” It’s an evidence-based list of medications that are potentially inappropriate for many adults age 65+, meaning they should be avoided when possible or used with extra caution.

You’ll learn:
- Why medication side effects often increase with age
- What the Beers Criteria is (and how it’s updated)
- The 5 key categories the Beers Criteria uses 
- How to look up your own medications in the Beers Criteria
- The common medication groups Dr. K especially watches for (brain-slowing meds, anticholinergics, sedatives, NSAIDs, aspirin for primary prevention, and fall-risk medications)
- What to ask your clinician or pharmacist to make medication use safer — including deprescribing conversations

Related resources:
AGS 2023 Beers Criteria (Journal article page):
https://agsjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jgs.18372

For more resources: https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/podcast/beers-criteria-explained-medications-older-adults-should-avoid/

text:
Sign up for Better Health While Aging’s newsletter to receive expert, practical health advice from board-certified geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH.: https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/for-older-adults/ 

If you (or your older loved ones) often take Tylenol, Advil, or aspirin for aches and pains, it’s essential to know which options are actually safe—and which could cause harm. Read more: https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/safest-otc-painkiller-aging-risks-of-nsaids/

In this episode of Better Health While Aging, board-certified geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH, breaks down what every older adult needs to know about over-the-counter painkillers. She explains how common medications like acetaminophen (Tylenol) and NSAIDs such as ibuprofen and naproxen (Advil, Aleve) affect aging bodies—and why some can increase the risk of bleeding, kidney problems, or stomach issues.

You’ll also learn:
The safest pain relief option for most older adults
When to avoid NSAIDs—and what to use instead
What to know about aspirin for pain and for prevention
Why topical creams and non-drug treatments can be a great alternative
What we know (and don’t know) about cannabinoids for pain
How to talk with doctors about better, safer pain management

If you’re dealing with arthritis, back pain, or chronic discomfort, this episode will help you make safer, more informed choices—and reduce the risk of serious side effects.

#OTCpainrelief #PainManagementSeniors #HelpingOlderParents #TylenolVsAdvil #SeniorHealthTips #BetterHealthForAging

Dr. Kernisan discusses common over the counter drugs like acetaminophen, also known as Tylenol, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, such as ibuprofen. She covers side effects of acetaminophen and other painkillers, offering senior care advice for older adults. This video offers health tips on pain management.

Find related resources here: https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/podcast/tylenol-advil-or-aspirin-safest-otc-painkillers-in-aging/

text:
Boosting bone density is one of the best ways to prevent fractures and protect independence as you age. In this episode, geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH, explains how bone density changes with aging, how osteoporosis and osteopenia are diagnosed, and proven ways that older adults can strengthen bones and lower fracture risk. She covers DEXA scans, T-scores, fragility fractures, and the best lifestyle measures that boost bone health. She also explains when osteoporosis medications may be worth considering.

Learn why both women and men should pay attention to bone density in later life, what to do if you’ve had a fracture, and which strategies are most effective for maintaining stronger, more fracture-resistant bones. This episode is especially helpful for older adults who want practical, evidence-based ways to age with better strength, mobility, and confidence. 

For more resources: https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/podcast/boosting-bone-density-in-aging/

Sign up for Better Health While Aging’s newsletter to receive practical health advice from board-certified geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH:

text:
Chronic pain affects nearly half of older adults — but that doesn’t mean it should be considered "normal." In this episode, geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH, explains how chronic pain in aging can be evaluated, what the most common causes are, and why a comprehensive, multidimensional treatment approach is often most effective.

Learn about non-drug options like physical therapy, acupuncture, and cognitive-behavioral therapy, as well as how to safely use medications like NSAIDs, antidepressants, and even opioids in select situations. You’ll also discover how conditions like arthritis, spinal stenosis, myofascial pain, fibromyalgia, and neuropathy contribute to ongoing pain — and what can be done to manage each.

Whether you’re an older adult or supporting someone with pain, this episode offers practical, research-backed insights to help you or your loved one feel and function better — without over-relying on risky medications.

text:
Urinary incontinence (bladder leaks) is common in later life, but it’s not “just aging,” and there ARE effective ways to improve it. In this episode, geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH explains the 5 main types of incontinence that affect women, what a good medical evaluation should include, and the most effective and safe incontinence treatments for older women.

You’ll learn how stress, urge (overactive bladder), mixed, overflow, and functional incontinence differ; what to know about pelvic floor dysfunction and prolapse; and where urogynecology fits in. We cover practical first steps (constipation care, timed voiding/bladder training, pelvic floor muscle work), low-dose vaginal estrogen, pessaries, and when to consider medications or procedures, plus special geriatric considerations for those who are very old, frail, or living with memory changes.

Whether you’re an older adult or helping a parent, this clear, step-by-step roadmap will help you discuss the right evaluation and safer options with your clinician, and regain confidence in daily life.

For more resources: https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/podcast/how-to-treat-urinary-incontinence-in-older-women/

Why evaluation matters: history, bladder diary, meds review, urinalysis, when pelvic exam helps
When to check post-void residual, assess pelvic floor, or refer to urogynecology
Red flags that merit specialist evaluation (e.g., visible blood in urine without UTI signs, neurologic symptoms, severe prolapse)
Lifestyle & behavioral therapy that works: constipation treatment, weight management, smoking cessation, caffeine/alcohol moderation, fluid strategies, pelvic floor muscle training (Kegels), and bladder training/timed voiding
Low-dose vaginal estrogen for postmenopausal urethral/vaginal tissue support
Pessaries and pelvic floor physical therapy

We cover practical first steps (constipation care, timed voiding/bladder training, pelvic floor muscle work), low-dose vaginal estrogen, pessaries, and when to consider medications or procedures, plus special geriatric considerations for those who are very old, frail, or living with memory changes.

Whether you’re an older adult or helping a parent, this clear, step-by-step roadmap will help you discuss the right evaluation and safer options with your clinician, and regain confidence in daily life.

Topics Covered
Female bladder & pelvic anatomy: how normal urination works
The 5 types of urinary incontinence in women (stress, urge/overactive bladder, mixed, overflow, functional)
Why evaluation matters: history, bladder diary, meds review, urinalysis, when pelvic exam helps
When to check post-void residual, assess pelvic floor, or refer to urogynecology
Red flags that merit specialist evaluation (e.g., visible blood in urine without UTI signs, neurologic symptoms, severe prolapse)
Lifestyle & behavioral therapy that works: constipation treatment, weight management, smoking cessation, caffeine/alcohol moderation, fluid strategies, pelvic floor muscle training (Kegels), and bladder training/timed voiding
Low-dose vaginal estrogen for postmenopausal urethral/vaginal tissue support
Pessaries and pelvic floor physical therapy

text:
Doctors often order blood tests during check-ups – but what do these results really mean as you get older?

In this episode, board-certified geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH breaks down the four most common blood tests ordered in older adults, including:
Complete Blood Count (CBC)
Basic Metabolic Panel (BMP)
Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP)
Lipid Panel (Cholesterol)

You’ll learn what these tests measure, what abnormal results might mean, and how to spot early signs of common health problems – like anemia, kidney issues, liver function changes, and high cholesterol.
This episode will help you:
Understand your blood test results with confidence
Know when to ask questions or follow up with your doctor
Avoid common misunderstandings about “normal” lab ranges
Be a more informed patient or caregiver

Perfect for proactive older adults—or anyone supporting an aging parent who’s managing chronic conditions or taking medications.

Dehydration is more than just feeling thirsty—especially as we get older. In this episode of the Better Health While Aging podcast, Dr. Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH, a board-certified geriatrician, explains how aging affects hydration and what you can do to protect yourself or a loved one.

Learn why older adults are more vulnerable to dehydration, how to recognize signs and symptoms that may be overlooked, how dehydration is actually diagnosed, and what practical treatment steps can help prevent serious health consequences. Dr. Kernisan also explains what to know about heat stroke and how to take precautions during heat waves. Whether you're navigating hot weather, illness, or daily life, this video will help you stay hydrated and healthier as you age.

Sign up for Better Health While Aging’s newsletter to receive expert, practical health advice from board-certified geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH.: https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/for-older-adults/

Find related resources here: https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/podcast/dehydration-and-heat-stroke-in-older-adults-symptoms-treatment-prevention/

Q&A: How to Prevent, Detect, & Treat Dehydration in Aging Adults: https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/qa-how-to-prevent-diagnose-treat-dehydration-aging-adults/

Topics Covered
What dehydration means and how it affects the body
Why older adults are more prone to dehydration
Common causes: medications, mobility, memory loss, incontinence
Symptoms to look for—and why they can be unreliable
How dehydration is diagnosed with lab tests
Treatment options for mild, moderate, and severe dehydration
Tips for preventing dehydration in daily life and hot weather
How to stay safe during heat waves

text:
Kidney disease becomes increasingly common with age, yet it’s often misunderstood, overlooked, or discovered only through routine lab tests. In this episode, geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH, explains how kidney function changes in later life, symptoms, types and stages of kidney disease, and how kidney disease should be managed for many older adults. 

You’ll learn how doctors assess kidney health using lab tests like eGFR and creatinine, what different CKD stages mean, and which causes are especially common in older adults, including high blood pressure, diabetes, dehydration, and certain medications. The video also walks through acute kidney injuries, treatment options, when referral to a kidney specialist may help, and what questions to ask your clinician so you can better understand your results and make informed decisions about your health as you age.

We’ll cover:
What your kidneys do and how kidney function is measured (eGFR, creatinine, BUN)
Chronic kidney disease vs acute kidney injury 
Symptoms of severe kidney dysfunction (fluid overload, high potassium, uremia)
Stages of kidney disease
Causes of kidney disease in older adults (blood pressure, diabetes, NSAIDs, more)
Managing kidney disease and when nephrology referral matters
Dialysis, transplant, and conservative (palliative) options for end stage kidney disease

Show notes and related resources: https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/podcast/kidney-disease-in-aging-causes-symptoms-treatment/

channelDescription:
If you're over 60 and want to stay sharp, active, and independent as you age, you’re in the right place. On this channel, geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH, breaks down complex health topics into clear, practical steps you can take based on the best of geriatrics and aging science.

From understanding medications and memory changes to improving nutrition and preventing falls, every video helps you age with clarity and confidence. To get weekly tips directly from Dr. K, sign up for her free newsletter below.

Supporting an aging parent or relative? Check out Dr. K’s companion channel, Helping Older Parents, where she shares videos specifically about caregiving and eldercare.

Disclaimer: All content is for educational purposes only and is not a substitute for personalized medical advice.

text:
Geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH, shares what’s new for the 2025–26 fall vaccine season, especially for adults over 60. She reviews the current COVID situation, the updated vaccine options (including Moderna’s mNexspike), and the latest CDC guidelines. Plus, key reminders on this year’s flu and RSV shots and practical tips for staying healthier this winter.

#covidvaccine #covidupdates #betterhealthwhileaging #flu #rsv #olderadults #geriatrician #immunization

Chapters:
00:00 Fall vaccines for older adults
01:05 COVID so far in 2025
06:20 Why fall vaccines matter
11:18 COVID vaccines for 2025–26
15:11 Moderna mNEXSPIKE and other options
23:37 Flu vaccines for 2025–26
25:16 What to know about RSV vaccines
26:32 How to reduce your chances of getting sick
29:47 Recap

text:
Managing Type 2 diabetes after 60 requires a different approach than in younger adults. In this episode of Better Health While Aging, geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH talks with diabetes researcher and UCSF geriatrician Sei Lee, MD MAS about how to individualize A1C goals, choose the safest medications, and avoid dangerous lows (hypoglycemia) in older adults.

They explain the pros and cons of today’s main diabetes treatments — metformin, SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, DPP-4 inhibitors, sulfonylureas, pioglitazone, and insulin — and how to balance benefits with risks depending on health, frailty, and life expectancy.
This conversation is designed for older adults living with diabetes, caregivers supporting aging parents, and anyone who wants safer, smarter diabetes care in later life.

Key Takeaways
Why diabetes care changes with aging and frailty
Safer A1C targets for older adults ( less than either 7.5%, 8%, 8.5%)
When tighter blood sugar control helps — and when it doesn’t
Risks of overtreatment and time to benefit considerations
When to use metformin first-line, and when to add newer drugs
Benefits of SGLT2s (kidney and heart protection) and GLP-1s (weight and appetite effects)
The role of insulin in geriatrics: basal vs mealtime
How to simplify regimens and prevent hypoglycemia
Using CGMs (continuous glucose monitors) in aging adults

Related Resources: https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/podcast/diabetes-best-safest-medications-for-seniors/

❓Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)
Q: What is a safe A1C goal for older adults?
 A: It depends on health status. In general, less than 7.5% for healthy older adults, less than 8% for those with multiple conditions, and  less than 8.5% for those with frailty or limited life expectancy.

Q: Which diabetes medications are safest for seniors?
 A: Metformin is usually first-line if kidney function is adequate. SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1s can offer heart and kidney benefits, but must be considered carefully. Sulfonylureas and insulin increase hypoglycemia risk.

Q: Why is overtreatment dangerous in older adults with diabetes?
 A: Aggressive lowering of blood sugar can cause hypoglycemia, leading to falls, confusion, or hospitalizations. Safer, individualized targets are recommended.

Q: What are the signs of hypoglycemia in seniors?
 A: Sweating, shakiness, confusion, dizziness, or even fainting. These can sometimes be harder to detect in older adults.

Q: Should older adults use continuous glucose monitors (CGMs)?
 A: CGMs can help some older adults, especially those on insulin, but may not be necessary for everyone. Decisions should consider cognitive status, caregiver support, and treatment goals.

text:
Age-related hearing loss is extremely common, but many older adults don’t realize how much it can affect communication, social connection, and brain health. In this episode, geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH, explains what to know about presbycusis, the medical term for age-related hearing loss, and why it’s worth identifying and treating hearing problems sooner rather than later.

You’ll learn how hearing loss often starts with difficulty understanding higher-pitched voices or hearing clearly in noisy places, why untreated hearing loss is linked to a higher risk of cognitive decline and dementia, and what steps can help you find out whether hearing loss may be affecting you.

Dr. K also covers practical options for treating hearing loss, including personal sound amplification products, over-the-counter hearing aids, and prescription hearing aids fitted by an audiologist. Plus, she shares what to do if you’ve tried hearing aids before and felt they didn’t work.

For more resources: https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/podcast/hearing-loss-in-aging-presbycusis/

Sign up for Better Health While Aging’s newsletter to receive practical health advice from board-certified geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH:

text:
Urinary incontinence (bladder leaks) and other urinary symptoms are very common in older men, but they’re not “just aging,” and there are effective ways to improve them. In this episode, geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH, explains how male bladder and pelvic anatomy, the prostate, and nerve function all affect urination in later life — and what to do if you’re having bothersome urinary symptoms or leaks.

You’ll learn what doctors mean by LUTS (lower urinary tract symptoms), how an enlarged prostate (BPH) contributes to urinary problems, and the 5 main types of incontinence that affect men: urgency, stress, mixed, overflow, and functional. Dr. Kernisan walks through what a good medical evaluation should include (not just “it’s your prostate”), which tests may help, and when symptoms should be treated as urgent rather than routine.

We also cover practical first steps (constipation care, timed voiding, double voiding, pelvic floor strategies) and safer use of medications for BPH and overactive bladder, including when to be cautious with anticholinergic drugs that affect thinking and bladder function. Special geriatric considerations for very old, frail men or those living with memory changes are discussed, including how families can help without assuming incontinence is inevitable.

Whether you’re an older man noticing urinary changes, or supporting an older loved one, this clear, step-by-step roadmap will help you talk with your clinician about the right evaluation and safer options, so you can worry less about the bathroom and more about daily life.

Further Resources can be found here: https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/podcast/urinary-incontinence-in-aging-men-causes-and-treatments/

Medications that can worsen LUTS or retention (anticholinergics, decongestants, diuretics)

text:
Diabetes is one of the most common chronic conditions in older adults, but managing it in aging requires a different approach. In this episode, geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH, explains what every older adult and their family should know about Type 2 diabetes, prediabetes, and blood sugar management in later life.

Learn about blood sugar and what “normal,” prediabetes, and diabetes mean for older adults. We compare Type 1 vs Type 2 diabetes in simple terms and highlight common diabetes symptoms, including signs of high blood sugar and low blood sugar (hypoglycemia). You’ll learn how diabetes is diagnosed and monitored – hemoglobin A1C, fasting glucose, and at-home blood sugar checks – so you can track results with confidence. We cover diabetes treatment for seniors: lifestyle tips, diet changes, and first-line medications like metformin for Type 2 diabetes. You’ll also hear why A1C targets should be tailored in older adults and how to avoid overtreatment and dangerous lows. By the end, you’ll know the key steps to manage Type 2 diabetes, control blood sugar, and reduce complications in aging.

This episode empowers older adults to better understand their blood sugar, ask the right questions during medical visits, and make informed choices about their treatment plan.

Whether you're living with diabetes, newly diagnosed, or supporting a loved one, this video offers a grounded, practical, and geriatric-specific overview of how to live better with diabetes in aging.

text:
Falls become more common with age, but they should never be dismissed as “just getting older.” In this episode, geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH, explains why older adults fall and the best ways to prevent falls. 

You’ll learn the most common causes of falling in later life and how geriatricians evaluate falls. Dr. Kernisan also explains the prevention approaches she uses the most, including physical therapy, strength and balance exercises for fall prevention, medication review, and home safety changes.

If you’ve had a recent fall, feel unsteady, or worry about falling, this video will help you better understand what to discuss with your health provider and what practical steps can reduce risk.

Related resources: 
CDC STEADI Stay Independent Brochure:
https://www.cdc.gov/steadi/pdf/STEADI-Brochure-StayIndependent-508.pdf

Videos Illustrating Otago Exercises for Fall Prevention
https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/otago-exercises-fall-prevention-videos/

For more resources: https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/podcast/how-to-prevent-falls-in-aging/

Sign up for Better Health While Aging’s newsletter to receive practical health advice from board-certified geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH:
https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/for-older-adults/

Age-related hearing loss, also called presbycusis, is very common after age 60 — but getting the right hearing loss treatment can feel confusing. Should you start with an audiologist? Are over-the-counter hearing aids enough? What about AirPods? And why do so many people say their expensive hearing aids “don’t work”?

In this episode of the Better Health While Aging video podcast, geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH, talks with audiologist Dr. Cliff Olson about today’s best and most affordable options for treating age-related hearing loss. Dr. Cliff is the founder of Applied Hearing Solutions Clinic and the creator of the well-established YouTube channel Dr. Cliff AuD, where he educates people about hearing loss, hearing aids, and audiology best practices.

You’ll learn how hearing loss should ideally be evaluated, what to look for in a high-quality hearing test, how audiologists interpret an audiogram, and when hearing loss might be managed with over-the-counter hearing aids (including AirPods) versus prescription hearing aids.

Dr. Cliff also explains one of the most important — and often missed — parts of hearing aid success: real ear measurement. This best-practice fitting method helps verify that hearing aids are actually programmed to match your hearing loss, so they can provide access to the speech sounds you’ve been missing.

If you’ve been told you need hearing aids, have tried hearing aids that ended up “in the drawer,” or simply want to understand your options before seeking care or investing in hearing aids, this conversation will help you become a more informed and proactive hearing healthcare consumer.

text:
Geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH, shares what’s new for the 2026–27 fall vaccine season, especially for adults 65 and older. She reviews the current COVID situation, the updated COVID vaccine options, and what’s changed in vaccine guidance this year. Plus, key updates on flu and RSV vaccines, including the new mRNA flu vaccine, and practical tips for reducing your risk of respiratory illness this winter.

For more resources: https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/podcast/covid-flu-fall-vaccines-2026/

Sign up for Better Health While Aging’s newsletter to receive practical health advice from board-certified geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH:

text:
Earwax is common, but as we get older it can sometimes build up enough to affect hearing — and it can also interfere with hearing aids.

Geriatrician Dr. Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH, talks with audiologist Dr. Cliff Olson, AuD, about what older adults should know about earwax, hearing loss, and safe earwax removal.

Learn what earwax is, why it can accumulate in the ear canal, and when it becomes a problem for hearing. Dr. Cliff also explains why earwax should be checked before assuming hearing aids are not working, and how earwax can affect hearing aids.

This conversation covers what can be done at home to help prevent earwax buildup, when over-the-counter earwax drops may be helpful, how to safely use cotton swabs at home, and how professionals remove earwax.

If you have hearing loss, wear hearing aids, or have been told you have earwax buildup, this video will help you understand safer ways to manage earwax and when to ask a healthcare professional or hearing care specialist for help.

For more resources: https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/podcast/earwax-removal-and-hearing-in-aging/

text:
With many Medicare plans being cancelled or raising premiums for next year, it’s more important than ever to review your Medicare coverage during Open Enrollment this fall. In this episode, geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH, is joined by geriatric social worker Michelle Allen, LCSW, to discuss Michelle’s experience trying out Chapter, a national free service that helps older adults find the best Medicare plan for them. Whether you’re shopping for a better Part D drug plan or need to find the Medicare Advantage plan that covers the doctors you want, Dr. K and Michelle review what to know, and explain your options for finding the best Medicare plan for you.

For FREE help learning about your best Medicare options, Dr. K recommends calling Chapter at 771-224-0630, or visit https://askchapter.org/betterhealth

What you’ll learn
- Why reviewing your Medicare plan yearly matters: premiums, benefits, and formularies often change — and many Medicare plans won’t renew for next year
- How to get started (review your insurance cards, online accounts, Annual Notices of Change) and what info to gather (prescriptions, doctors, pharmacy, preferred hospital).
- Comparing your options: Medicare.gov Plan Finder, SHIP, local brokers — plus a newer phone-based, free help option (Chapter) that can check both your medications and your providers across virtually all plans.

#Medicare  #MedicareAdvantage #SeniorHealth #BetterHealthWhileAging #OpenEnrollment #RetirementPlanning #HealthInsurance

About Chapter:
You call and speak with a licensed Medicare advisor who reviews your doctors, prescriptions, and preferences, generates a tailored list of plan options, and can email details so you can decide at your pace. Advisors are salaried and do not know which plans pay the company more or less, which means there’s no incentive to encourage you to pick anything other than the plan that’s best for you.

For FREE help learning about your best Medicare options, Dr. K recommends calling Chapter at 771-224-0630, or visit https://askchapter.org/betterhealth

Related resources: https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/podcast/save-money-on-medicare-and-chapter-medicare-review/

Affiliate disclosure
Dr. Kernisan declined to be paid to make this video. After evaluating Chapter, she agreed to become an affiliate. This means that if you choose to use Chapter’s free service through her referral, Better Health While Aging may receive a commission that helps support our educational work. Thank you!

text:
Vitamin B12 plays a crucial role in keeping the brain, nerves, and energy levels functioning well, but not all B12 supplements are created equal. So which type of Vitamin B12 to take? In this episode, geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD, takes a closer look at the two most common forms— methylcobalamin and cyanocobalamin —and explains how the body processes them, their effectiveness for older adults, and what the latest research really says. There’s a lot of debate about which form is better, but the truth isn’t so simple. 

Dr. Kernisan breaks down the key differences and shares a practical, science-based perspective to help you decide which type of B12 may be best for you or your aging loved ones. If you’ve ever been unsure about B12 supplements, this episode will provide the clarity needed to make an informed choice, especially if you want to treat or prevent vitamin B12 deficiency.

If you or someone you care for is dealing with fatigue, memory issues, or nerve-related symptoms, understanding B12 and making the right supplementation choice is essential. Dr. Kernisan’s goal in this episode is to provide clear, evidence-based guidance so you can feel confident in managing B12 levels for better health as you age.

Have you been diagnosed with osteoporosis, had a fragility fracture, or been told you need medication to boost your bone density?

In this episode, geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH, explains what older adults should know about osteoporosis medications, including when they are usually recommended, how they work, and what side effects or precautions to discuss with your health provider.

You’ll learn how osteoporosis is diagnosed using a DEXA scan and T-score, why fragility fractures matter, and why medications are generally recommended for osteoporosis rather than osteopenia. Dr. K also explains the most commonly used first-line medications, including bisphosphonates such as alendronate/Fosamax and yearly IV zoledronic acid/Reclast, plus other options such as raloxifene/Evista, denosumab/Prolia, teriparatide/Forteo, abaloparatide/Tymlos, and romosozumab/Evenity.

This video also covers what to know about bisphosphonate “drug holidays,” why bone density should be monitored during treatment, what lifestyle measures can support bone health, and what to ask your doctor before starting — or declining — medication.

For more resources: https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/podcast/osteoporosis-medications-explained/

text:
Could your medications be increasing your risk of falling? Probably! That’s why geriatricians ALWAYS review medications, to help older adults prevent falls. 

In this episode, geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH, explains 10 types of medications to check if you’ve been falling, feeling unsteady, or are concerned about fall risk. You’ll learn how certain medications can affect balance, reflexes, alertness, blood pressure, and blood sugar — and why these effects can become especially important in later life.

Dr. Kernisan also explains what to do if you discover you’re taking a medication that may contribute to falls. Rather than stopping medications on your own, learn how to work with your healthcare provider to consider whether a medication can be stopped, switched to a safer alternative, or reduced to the lowest effective dose.

You’ll also get practical questions to ask your doctor or pharmacist and learn why medication review should be part of a more comprehensive approach to preventing falls.

For more resources: https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/podcast/medications-that-can-cause-falls-in-aging/

text:
Managing high blood pressure (hypertension) is one of the most important ways to protect your brain, heart, and kidneys as you age. In this episode, geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH, explains the best ways to lower blood pressure in older adults, using both lifestyle changes and medications that are safe and effective for aging bodies.

#highbloodpressure, #bloodpressuretips, #dashdiet, #seniorhealth, #agingwell, #betterhealthwhileaging

You’ll learn about the DASH diet, sodium and potassium intake, types of blood pressure medications (like calcium channel blockers and ACE inhibitors), and how to decide on the right blood pressure goals for your age and health status. Dr. Kernisan also explains why accurate blood pressure measurement is key, especially when monitoring at home, and highlights common issues like orthostatic hypotension and sensitivity to medication in frail older adults.

Whether you’re an older adult or a health professional, this episode provides science-based, practical advice to help you lower blood pressure and reduce long-term health risks.

You can find more resources here: https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/podcast/how-to-lower-blood-pressure-and-treat-hypertension/

help with high blood pressure. That is
actually true. This has been studied uh
several times and in a meta analysis uh
they concluded that in people with high
blood pressure increasing the potassium
intake reduced systolic blood pressure
by 5 mm of mercury. Um now no reduction
in blood pressure was seen in people who
had normal blood pressure. So this is
another thing that works in people who
are hypertensive not so much in uh those
people who are already uh at a level
that's close to normal or optimal. So
how can you increase potassium? So
potassium is naturally found in lots of
fruits and vegetables. So increasing
your intake through more fruits and
vegetables is one way to do this. That
is potentially part of the reason why
the DASH diet works. But uh there it is
also possible in some cases to take
potassium supplements. That's sometimes
recommended especially in people who
have low blood potassium levels or who
are on medications that lower their
potassium uh levels because there are
some medications that do that. Uh and
then there are also salt substitutes
that uh involve potassium chloride. So
if you are thinking of those, what's
important to know, especially for older
adults, is you want to be very careful
with those kinds of supplements or salt
substitutes. If you have any kidney
disease, and that's because when people
have kidney disease, their potassium
tends to go up. And if your potassium is
too high, that can actually uh interfere
with your muscle function and uh be
dangerous. you know, that's actually a
method of lethal injection is to give
people a lot of potassium because when
you make people's potassium levels
really really high, their heart starts
to skitter and um will eventually um
skitter and go kind of nuts and then
stop. So, you do want to be careful with
potassium supplements or salt
substitutes if there is any kidney
disease or if the person is taking
medications that affect electrolytes and
those include many diuretics and some
blood pressure
medications. And then what about any
other lifestyle approaches for blood
pressure? Um so there are some
approaches that have been less
rigorously studied but they also seem
likely to help reduce blood pressure.
They include things like yoga,
meditation and mindfulness, uh stress
reduction, treatment of insomnia,
quitting tobacco. So uh if you are
wondering about well if I do these will
it help my blood pressure? Probably you
know would be my guess. These are all
things that in a in a way kind of reduce
a state of chronic stress. uh and help
people be uh more relaxed and that tends
to lower blood pressure. Uh we just
don't know quite as much um about it,
but I would recommend it because these
things are all good for your health for
many other reasons. So that's lifestyle
measures for blood pressure. And
lifestyle measures are great, but the
truth is that often they are not enough.
They can be hard to implement. They they
require often effort. They require
commitment. They require sticking to it
for weeks or months to um well first of
all many of them you need to do it for
at least probably two weeks to see if
it's having an effect um on your blood
pressure and then you need to be ready
to continue doing it indefinitely and
that can be a lot. So let me now talk
about medications. Um now in geriatrics
we are often fans of you know less is
more. We often try to minimize
medications but I have to say
medications do work extremely well for
high blood pressure. So this is a
situation where we are uh more likely
actually to use medications. Now we're
often using smaller doses than other
providers. We're not aiming for as low a
goal as the cardiologists do. But I know
many people who are a little leerary of
medications and I think that's justified
and this is one case where we have lots
and lots of evidence of medications
working quite well and improving uh
outcomes. So first of all, medications
in almost everyone will lower blood
pressure and we see an effect generally
within uh
days and then not only do they lower the
blood pressure but they lower those bad
health outcomes that are the result of
high blood pressure and this has been
shown over and over again in randomized
uh trials such as the sprint trial which
I mentioned in the previous video you
know one of the landmark trials of blood
pressure control in uh older adults.
There are others too. There are trials
called Shep and Hyet uh that have shown
this too. So uh so we we have seen that
when we treat people with blood pressure
medications and we successfully bring
down their blood pressure within just a
few years you can see reductions in
cardiovascular events in strokes and in
uh
mortality. So again I think lifestyle
measures are great. I think we are
underusing them and it is often hard for
people to reach their goal blood
pressure with lifestyle measures alone.
So I think it's important to be open to
considering medication uh especially if
your systolic blood pressure is above
150 because in most cases even though
many blood pressure medications do have
side effects either common side effects
or occasional bad effects in certain
people despite that in many cases um
possibly even most cases the likely
benefits of medication treatment
outweigh the risks. So what are the
medications that we usually consider
when we are trying to treat high blood
pressure? Uh this has been studied a lot
in randomized trials. So there are
expert guidelines and sort of firstline
treatment recommendations that are well
established. Uh and this is what they
are. So for initial treatment with uh a
single drug or possibly sometimes if
people's blood pressure is quite high
they might start right off the bat with
two drugs. But there are three key
classes of blood pressure medication
that are considered firstline therapy.
They have a good wellestablished
uh track record. So unless there's a
compelling reason to not use any of
them, if somebody is diagnosed with high
blood pressure, this is where a health
provider should be starting. And those
three types of blood pressure medication
are one is long acting dihydropodine
calcium channel blockers. I know it's a
mouthful. Uh so these are medications
I'll go through um a few more examples
in a moment but a common example would
be amloopene you know the brand name is
Norvasque. Another uh class of drug that
is considered a first-line therapy is a
thazide diuretic um such as
hydrochloroioide. And then a third class
or you could say this is class three and
four is an ACE inhibitor or an ARB. Um
so I'm going to explain this type of
medication in a moment. These two are
extremely closely related. You would
usually use either one or the other, not
both of them together. And a common
example of an ACE inhibitor would be uh
leinopril or of an ARB would be
something like low sartan. So sometimes
we do also start with combination
treatments. Um there is some evidence
that that can be a little bit more
effective. The downside is that if
somebody's having side effects or it's
not agreeing with them, then it's a
little bit more complicated to figure
out, you know, which medication is the
issue. But if we are going to start with
combo treatment, this would involve
using two of the three above drug types.
That is what is considered kind of like
the initial way that you are supposed to
attempt to manage high blood pressure.
Now, you may be thinking, well, I have
high blood pressure and my medication
isn't one of these. Um well there are
many other medications that affect blood
pressure and some of them are
specifically recommended for people who
have certain types of heart or kidney
conditions or in other cases people
haven't tolerated the initial uh set of
medications that are recommended for
first-line therapy or some people have
such difficult to manage high blood
pressure that we just end up having to
go to you know sort of the the second
line therapy medications as well. Let me
now talk about those uh key types of
blood pressure medication in a little
bit more depth. So first of all, calcium
channel blockers for blood pressure.
What we want is the lung acting
dihydropiritine calcium channel
blockers. There's another type of
calcium channel blocker uh that acts
less on your blood vessels and more on
your heart. It's sometimes used to treat
you know atrial fibrillation or
conditions like that. But um the long
acting dihydropitine ones most commonly
used in the United States would be
amloopene, foopine, nephipene. The brand
names are Norvas, Plendil and then the
fetipene goes by both procardia and
adelat. These act mainly by relaxing
your blood vessel walls. And um the
advantage of these is that they uh don't
really affect electrolytes. Many blood
pressure medications affect electrolytes
but these do not. So that means less lab
monitoring required which can be nice.
And then a common side effect is that
they can cause leg swelling at times.
Next, thide diuretics for high blood
pressure. So, the main one we use in the
United States is
hydrochloroioide. Uh, another one that
is used especially in other countries is
chloraladone. Now, there are other types
of diuretics that exist as well, you
know, such as loop diuretics such as
fioamide often prescribed for people who
have heart failure. Uh, that's not the
same kind of diuretic. So these are
thazide diuretics and the way they act
is they increase sodium and water
excretion in the kidneys. Generally
these are well tolerated but they do
require monitoring of electrolytes
because while this medication is
changing how you excrete sodium it's
also affecting how your kidneys process
certain other uh electrolytes. So some
common side effects I mean the way this
works is it does make people pee more.
That can be an issue for some older
adults especially if they are already
struggling to manage uh their urination
and their continents and then it can
lower blood electrolyte levels
especially potassium levels, sodium
levels and magnesium levels. This kind
of diuretic also tends to increase blood
levels of calcium. This is sometimes
considered a good thing for people who
have osteoporosis but it also increases
uric acid which can exacerbate a
condition such as gout. Despite these
side effects, these medications are
often used including in older adults and
generally do have a good track record.
And then uh let me now talk about ACE
inhibitors and then I'll talk about
ARBs. So ACE inhibitors uh include
medications such as bonazipril uh
leinopril and many many more. If you
Google you know list of ACE inhibitors
you'll you'll see lots of them. And the
way these act is that ACE inhibitors
inhibit an enzyme that is called ACE
which is an angotensin converting enzyme
basically and so that reduces levels of
uh a substance in the body a vasoc
constricting substance so that means it
tightens up your blood vessels that is
called angotensin 2 and um so ACE
inhibits the conversion of I think it's
angotensin one to angotensin 2 and so
you have less angotensin 2 and so your
blood vessels won't stay as constricted
as they otherwise would. This is another
medication that we have a pretty good
track record on um and is often well
tolerated, but it does require
monitoring of electrolytes and kidney
function. An ACE inhibitor almost always
raises somebody's potassium a bit and
raises some it will usually raise their
creatinine a little bit which is a
measure of kidney function. And those
small changes are expected and are okay.
we basically monitor to make sure it's
not a large change. So these will tend
to increase potassium levels and then
side effects ACE inhibitors can also
have certain side effects that are
specific to them. So one is cough
actually uh and another one is
angioadeema where people get face
swelling. So both these side effects are
not something we expect to see in
everybody. They affect a minority of
people though. And if people are having
that side effect, generally we're going
to want to switch them to an ARB, uh,
which is a related, uh, drug that I'm
about to tell you about, but doesn't
have those side effects. And then we're
generally looking out for
problematically high potassium levels
and significantly worsen kidney
function. So what's interesting about
ACE inhibitors is despite the fact that
they make your kidney function a little
worse, they actually have been shown to
be renotective. They actually protect
the kidneys from ongoing damage from
conditions like diabetes and they also
help protect the heart when the heart
has been previously damaged. So they're
often actually a good choice if people
have diabetes or for certain heart
conditions such as having heart failure.
Uh so it's a little counterintuitive,
but if people have those conditions
along with their high blood pressure,
then we'll be especially likely to want
to use either an ACE or an ARB because
they can be kind of interchangeable. So
ARBs ARBs are kind of working in a very
similar mechanism of action. What they
do is they block the action of that
angotensin 2. They are an andotensin
receptor blocker. So both the ACE
inhibitors and the ARBs result in a
decreased effect of that angotensin 2
just through slightly different
mechanisms. So, uh, similar to ACE
inhibitors, they're generally well
tolerated, but also require a little
monitoring of electrolytes and kidney
function. With ARBs, we do expect to see
a little rise in potassium and a little
worsening of kidney function. But
otherwise, ARBs do not have this uh side
effect of cough or angioadema. So, with
those, we're generally just again
monitoring potassium and kidney
function. And um, ARBs are also
renoprotective and cardoprotective. So
also often a good choice if people have
diabetes, heart failure or certain other
conditions. So generally when it comes
to managing high blood pressure, we
would use either an ACE inhibitor or an
ARB. Uh generally not both of them
together. So if we're doing that two out
of three drug combination, you would not
expect to see the ACE inhibitor and ARB
together. It would be one of those two
along with something else such as a
calcium channel blocker. Now let me
briefly speak to another type of blood
pressure medication which you may have
heard about before which are beta
blockers. What about beta blockers? So
beta blockers there was a time actually
when I was in medical school beta
blockers were prescribed for primary
hypertension all the time. So this is a
type of blood pressure medication that
works by slowing down your heart rate.
And some commonly prescribed ones
include mtopriol, a tunnel, carvdalol.
The brand names there are uh Toprell,
uh, Tenorin and Coragg. So they were for
a time often used for primary
hypertension, but what was found through
a lot of research was that they were not
great for that, especially not in older
adults. So they are no longer
recommended for the treatment of
isolated hypertension. If a person has
hypertension without having another type
of heart condition for which beta
blockers are good, they probably
shouldn't be on a beta blocker. uh beta
blockers are definitely helpful when it
comes to certain heart conditions,
especially heart failure or recent heart
attacks. Otherwise, um certainly at
UCSF, a lot of primary care providers a
while back made an effort to transition.
There are patients who have primary
hypertension from a beta blocker to one
of those other three drugs that I
mentioned. So, let me now speak to what
is most important in my opinion for
blood pressure treatment. So studies
have found that it's really the attained
goal blood pressure you get to that's
most important, not which of those three
drugs. But what's important is that you
get accurate blood pressure measurements
initially and as you are treating to see
what's going on. You want to use good
technique. Combining home measurements
with office measurements is best. Please
always include your heart rate with your
blood pressure measurements. You want to
take your medications as directed or if
you are supporting an older frailer
person, you will want to make sure they
are taking their medication. This comes
up sometimes with some of my uh older
patients, especially if they're older,
live alone and maybe have been having
some memory problems, right? Sometimes
people's blood pressure is out of
control and it's because they haven't
been taking the medication. So, we don't
want to be changing or increasing the
medication if the issue is that they
haven't been taking it. If you are in
treatment, especially if there's been a
change or you've just started, you want
to ask what kind of high or low blood
pressure should prompt a call to your
doctor. And then you want to get
followup and adjust treatments. A
follow-up in two to four weeks to check
blood pressure, to check for side
effects, and adjust medications is often
reasonable. Let me now speak to some
special considerations that affect older
adults, especially once people get into
their 80s and older. So, what we know is
that as people age, systolic blood
pressure tends to go up and diastolic
actually tends to go down. This is
related to the stiffening of the
arteries that affects most people as
they get older. Really, it affects
everybody. It's just a question of how
fast and when. So as people get into
their 70s, 80s, 90s, uh it's very common
for them to have something that is
sometimes called isolated systolic
hypertension where the top number is
very high but the bottom number, the
diastolic is quite low. So some of the
blood pressure management issues that
come up in later life that we are often
dealing with in geriatrics but that are
also affecting other primary care
providers. One, as people get much
older, their blood pressure can be
extremely variable where sometimes it is
really really high and other times it is
barely high. Uh they can have quite low
diastolic such as 60 or sometimes lower.
People sometimes are asking me how low
is too low. You know what I say is how
is the person feeling you know when they
stand up. If they stand up and they feel
weak or dizzy you know that's probably
too low. Uh if their diastolic is 55 but
they're feeling fine even when they
stand up then I would worry a little
less about it. As people get older, they
tend to become quite sensitive to blood
pressure drugs or to their side effects.
So, they might need more caution and
monitoring because of that. Another
issue is that a lot of people might have
a low systolic blood pressure when they
stand up. And especially as you get
older and frailer, that lower pressure
might either mean that you have less
blood flow to your brain. And we see
some people who seem to actually
sometimes get a little bit more confused
um if not lightaded uh when they're
standing when their blood pressure is
low. Or there are some people whose
blood pressure drops a full 20 points
when they stand up. This is something
that is called orthostatic hypotension.
It means dropping your blood pressure
when you change position. It's uh a
known issue that is very common in older
adults especially if they are on blood
pressure medications. and it can
increase the risk of falls. If a person
stands up and for the first few minutes
their blood pressure drops 20 points. Uh
and this is often happening because the
mechanisms you have in your body that
are supposed to make adjustments to keep
your blood pressure stable because when
you stand up blood your your blood falls
into your legs is basically it's what it
wants to do unless your body very
quickly makes adjustments and when we're
young our body is good at making those
adjustments and as we get older it gets
worse at that. Uh so that's another
issue that we're often checking for in
geriatrics as well. So in geriatrics
especially for adults who are aged 80 or
older or are frail. Uh we tend to first
of all aim for a solid blood pressure
goal of 140. It was shown in sprint
senior which was in people you know age
75 plus that aiming for that lower blood
pressure goal of 120 instead of 140 did
improve outcomes. So we know it works
for older adults. uh we just generally
first try to get to 140 and then really
check and make sure see how the person
is doing before we aim for lower and
again I talked a little bit about sprint
in the previous video but you know there
were many frail older people who were
actually excluded from a sprint
including people with Alzheimer's and
other forms of uh dementia uh so we you
know tend to go more of the line of you
know the European guidelines and aim for
systolic 140 we do a lot of monitoring
for signs of over treatments I And if
somebody comes in to see me and sitting
down, their systolic blood pressure is
less than 120. I don't say, "Yay." I get
concerned. I say, "Are you feeling okay
when you stand up? Let's check your
blood pressure when you stand up. How
much blood pressure medication are you
on? Do you really need to be on quite as
much? Should we think about scaling back
a little bit?" Uh, I think it's good to
treat blood pressure. I'm just not
always convinced that we need to be
super aggressive about it, especially if
there have been any concerns about fall
or frailty. So again uh we're quite
likely to check for orthostatic
hypotension. We will also check on
medication adherence especially before
increasing medication uh dosages
especially when it comes to people who
live alone or have had any uh issues
with their memory. We also check often
on electrolytes and kidney uh function.
Many people as they get older are more
prone to have poor kidney function or to
develop electrolyte imbalances in
response to medications. And then uh I'm
a big fan of home blood pressure
monitoring. You know, the more data
points the better. And in general, we
tend to manage blood pressure in light
of the greater picture of the person's
health, their overall health status,
their goals of medical care, their other
health conditions. Uh some people have
lots of health problems going on at the
same time, and it just may not make
sense to be really aggressive about
their blood pressure control at that uh
time. Some people don't want to be on
lots and lots of medication if that's
what it takes to manage their blood
pressure. And maybe we'll decide that
it's reasonable for them to be kind of,
you know, have a systolic blood pressure
of around 150 depending on what else is
going on with their health and uh how
much longer we expect they are likely to
live. So to recap, how to lower blood
pressure. So when it comes to lifestyle,
the DASH diet is good. Low sodium DASH
diet can be even better. So that would
involve a high intake of vegetables,
fruits, and the original dash was
low-fat dairy. Also, low intake of
snacks, sweets, meats, saturated fat,
and total fat. If you want to go a
dietary approach, I would say change the
diet. Remember to be your own test
subject. Change your diet. Don't change
anything else. Actually, check your
blood pressure every day for 2 weeks.
See what happens. Uh, that should do it.
Exercise also helps lower blood pressure
and is otherwise amazing for your aging
health. I especially recommend strength
exercises, but some aerobic exercise is
good too for your aging health. And I
have a whole video about aging and
exercise if you want to learn more about
that. Reducing alcohol intake is another
thing to consider. It can help with
blood pressure and also has other
benefits for heart health and likely
reduces your cancer risk as well. And
then uh in terms of lowering blood
pressure through medications,
medications are a very effective way to
lower blood pressure. Generally safe
enough, generally the benefits outweigh
the risks. For initial treatment with a
single drug, three classes are
considered first-line therapy. So that
would be the calcium channel blockers
such as enloopene, thazide diuretics
such as
hydrochloroioide and ACE inhibitors or
ARBs such as leinopril or loartan. Some
people will also uh might start with a
combination treatment. There are
combination pills actually that can be
given which is convenient or a small
dose of two of those three types. And
then uh just remember that many other
drugs affect blood pressure. You might
be prescribed something different
especially if you have a certain type of
heart condition or kidney condition as
well. And then in terms of you know how
to lower blood pressure, you want to
make sure the blood pressure is measured
accurately. You want to make sure your
health providers have checked for
secondary hypertension and treated or
removed any causes including medications
that might be aggravating your blood
pressure. You want to decide on what
goal blood pressure is being targeted.
You want to discuss and implement
lifestyle changes that lower blood
pressure. Start or adjust treatment with
blood pressure medication, especially if
systolic blood pressure is above 150.
Follow-up is key. Make a plan to follow
up to assess the effect and side effects
of the blood pressure treatment. adjust
treatment until gold blood pressure is
reached. And then optional is to
reassess the goal blood pressure,
especially if you started off with a
goal that wasn't uh less than 130 over
80. If you reach your goal, if that
first goal was 140 over 80, uh you can
reassess and maybe decide to aim for a
lower goal. So, thank you so much for
watching. And if you found this video
podcast helpful, if you're here on
YouTube, please go ahead and subscribe.
It does help more people find the
channel. If you've been listening to the
audio version on the podcast feed,
please come and take a look at the video
if you get a chance. You'll see my key
points being displayed on the screen.
So, thank you again and I look forward
to seeing you all again on a future
episode of the Better Health while Aging
Video Podcast.

Sign up for Better Health While Aging’s newsletter to receive expert, practical health advice from board-certified geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH.: https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/for-older-adults/

Low blood pressure can sound like a good thing, but in older adults, it may lead to symptoms like dizziness, fatigue, or even falls. In this episode of Better Health While Aging, geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH, explains what counts as low blood pressure, why it happens in aging, and how to recognize warning signs — especially if you’re caring for aging parents or experiencing these issues yourself. 

Dr. Kernisan also discusses orthostatic hypotension, a specific type of low blood pressure that happens when standing up, and outlines a practical, step-by-step approach to managing low BP. This includes reviewing medications, monitoring at home, and understanding how blood pressure goals may shift in older age. 

If you or a loved one have been told your blood pressure is “too low” or you’ve experienced lightheadedness or fainting, this episode will help you better understand what to do next, and how to manage this safely and effectively. 

For more resources: https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/podcast/hypotension-and-low-blood-pressure-in-aging/

Sign up for Better Health While Aging’s newsletter to receive expert, practical health advice from board-certified geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH.: https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/fo...

Low blood pressure can sound like a good thing, but in older adults, it may lead to symptoms like dizziness, fatigue, or even falls. In this episode of Better Health While Aging, geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH, explains what counts as low blood pressure, why it happens in aging, and how to recognize warning signs — especially if you’re caring for aging parents or experiencing these issues yourself. 

Dr. Kernisan also discusses orthostatic hypotension, a specific type of low blood pressure that happens when standing up, and outlines a practical, step-by-step approach to managing low BP. This includes reviewing medications, monitoring at home, and understanding how blood pressure goals may shift in older age. 

If you or a loved one have been told your blood pressure is “too low” or you’ve experienced lightheadedness or fainting, this episode will help you better understand what to do next, and how to manage this safely and effectively.

text:
Hospital delirium is a sudden change in thinking and attention that affects many hospitalized older adults. It may cause confusion, agitation, hallucinations, unusual sleepiness, or difficulty following a conversation, and it can sometimes be mistaken for dementia.

Geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH, explains what hospital delirium is, why older adults are more vulnerable, and how it can be prevented, recognized, and treated.

Learn about common triggers, including infections, surgery, anesthesia, dehydration, sleep disruption, medication side effects, pain, constipation, restraints, and the unfamiliar hospital environment. Dr. Kernisan also explains the difference between hyperactive and hypoactive delirium, how delirium is diagnosed, why family members can help identify changes from baseline, and what to expect during recovery.

For more resources: https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/podcast/hospital-delirium-in-older-adults/

If you or an aging parent has been told you have a slow heart rate, you might be wondering: Is it dangerous? Will I need a pacemaker? What does this mean for my health going forward? #pacemaker #heartrate 

In this episode of Better Health While Aging, Dr. Leslie Kernisan is joined by cardiologist Dr. Cara Pellegrini to explain what older adults and families really need to know about bradycardia (slow heart rate) and pacemakers.

You’ll learn:
What a slow heart rate actually means in aging
Which symptoms—like fatigue, dizziness, or confusion—could signal a problem
How doctors decide when a pacemaker is the right treatment
What to expect before, during, and after a pacemaker procedure
The difference between traditional and leadless pacemakers
How pacemakers are monitored and maintained over time

They also talk about how this condition is different for frail older adults or those in their 80s and 90s, and how to approach decision-making around treatment and quality of life.

Whether you’ve just been diagnosed or are trying to understand care options for a loved one, this video offers clear, practical answers to help you feel more confident about what comes next.

Watch now to better understand slow heart rates in aging—and when treatment really matters.

text:
High blood pressure, or hypertension, is one of the most common health issues in older adults, but many people don’t fully understand what it means or when it should be treated. In this episode, Dr. Leslie Kernisan explains what blood pressure numbers really mean, what’s normal BP and what’s considered too high, and why managing hypertension is so important for long-term health.

Important Blood Pressure Studies: What to Know About SPRINT-Senior & Other Research: https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/blood-pressure-study-sprint-senior/

Dr. Kernisan also talks about what causes high blood pressure, why it often goes unnoticed, and how it can increase the risk of strokes, heart disease, and kidney problems. She explains the differences between U.S. and European blood pressure guidelines, how to get accurate blood pressure readings, and what blood pressure older adults should aim for.

If you or a loved one have high blood pressure, this episode will help you understand when treatment is needed, how to monitor blood pressure at home, and what steps to take to reduce health risks.

Find related resources here: https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/podcast/what-is-high-blood-pressure-in-aging/

text:
Liver problems are common in later life, but they tend to stay quiet, so damage can build for years before anything feels wrong.

In this episode, geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH, covers seven warning signs of a struggling liver. 

She also explains the most common causes of liver trouble in older adults, including fatty liver disease, alcohol, medications and supplements, hepatitis C, and gallstones – and shares practical steps to protect your liver and the questions to ask your health provider about your lab results.

For more resources: https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/podcast/7-warning-signs-struggling-liver/

Liver problems are common in later life, but they tend to stay quiet, so damage can build for years before anything feels wrong.

In this episode, geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH, covers seven warning signs of a struggling liver. 

She also explains the most common causes of liver trouble in older adults, including fatty liver disease, alcohol, medications and supplements, hepatitis C, and gallstones – and shares practical steps to protect your liver and the questions to ask your health provider about your lab results.

For more resources: https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/po...

Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are one of the most common infections affecting older adults. text:
Can a urinary tract infection (UTI) cause memory loss?  Geriatricians Leslie Kernisan, MD and Chrissy Kistler, MD, continue their discussion, focusing on how to know when confusion or weakness is being caused by UTIs, and how to diagnose and treat UTIs in more vulnerable older adults, such as those in nursing homes. Discover how UTIs can mimic confusion or memory loss and learn why geriatricians always consider whether there is asymptomatic bacteriuria (“colonized bladder”) in these cases. The geriatricians also cover managing urinary tract infections in older adults with Alzheimer’s and related dementia, explain when to use antibiotics, and discuss how to prevent recurrent UTIs.

Watch Part 1 Here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0sC4L1ALRGs

Find related resources here:  https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/podcast/utis-in-alzheimers-dementia-and-nursing-homes/

text:
Geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD, talks with social worker and Aging Life Care Professional Michelle Allen, LCSW, about the crucial updates and insights into Medicare coverage that everyone over 65 should be aware of. With Medicare Open Enrollment approaching, it's vital to understand your options and ensure you're getting the best value for your healthcare needs. They also explain what to do during this time to keep out-of-pocket costs lower for the coming year.

Learn about the different parts of Medicare, including Medicare Advantage and Part D, and discover important changes coming in Medicare 2025 that could impact your coverage. The discussion also highlights a cap on prescription drug costs and provides practical steps for navigating the enrollment process and resources for assistance.

Find related resources here: https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/podcast/checking-parts-of-medicare-and-open-enrollment/

translatedText:
Geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD, talks with social worker and Aging Life Care Professional Michelle Allen, LCSW, about the crucial updates and insights into Medicare coverage that everyone over 65 should be aware of. With Medicare Open Enrollment approaching, it's vital to understand your options and ensure you're getting the best value for your healthcare needs. They also explain what to do during this time to keep out-of-pocket costs lower for the coming year.

Learn about the different parts of Medicare, including Medicare Advantage and Part D, and discover important changes coming in Medicare 2025 that could impact your coverage. The discussion also highlights a cap on prescription drug costs and provides practical steps for navigating the enrollment process and resources for assistance.

Find related resources here: https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/po...

Want to learn more about getting guidance with YOUR aging parents from Dr. K and her handpicked team of professional eldercare experts? Learn more about Dr. K's Helping Older Parents programs here: https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/he...

If you're over 60 and want to stay sharp, active, and independent as you age, you’re in the right place. On this channel, geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH, breaks down complex health topics into clear, practical steps you can take based on the best of geriatrics and aging science.

Planning for a healthy and successful aging journey is crucial, and geriatrician Dr. Leslie Kernisan, MD, shares key insights on how to prepare for aging well. In this video, you'll discover actionable steps to prevent common aging issues, delay chronic conditions, and improve quality of life as you age. Learn expert advice on anticipating end-of-life challenges and maintaining independence, wellness, and joy in your later years.

Topics Covered:
How to plan for successful aging and stay healthy in later life
Preventing common senior health problems and managing chronic illness
Strategies to enhance quality of life for seniors and caregivers
Insights into the most common end-of-life pathways and what families need to know
How to plan for a stage of eldercare and interdependence

Whether you're planning for yourself or supporting a loved one, these strategies will empower you to take proactive steps for a fulfilling aging experience. text:
Anemia is a common issue for older adults, but many don’t realize that iron supplements aren’t always the right treatment. Dr. Leslie Kernisan, a geriatrician, sheds light on what really causes anemia, how it’s diagnosed, and the best ways to treat it. Important information about symptoms to watch for, questions to ask your doctor, and the 10 most common causes of anemia in aging adults. Anemia is not just a diagnosis — it’s often a sign of an underlying health issue.

channelDescription:
If you're over 60 and want to stay sharp, active, and independent as you age, you’re in the right place. On this channel, geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH, breaks down complex health topics into clear, practical steps you can take based on the best of geriatrics and aging science.

From understanding medications and memory changes to improving nutrition and preventing falls, every video helps you age with clarity and confidence. To get weekly tips directly from Dr. K, sign up for her free newsletter below.

Supporting an aging parent or relative? Check out Dr. K’s companion channel, Helping Older Parents, where she shares videos specifically about caregiving and eldercare.

Disclaimer: All content is for educational purposes only and is not a substitute for personalized medical advice.

text:
Geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD, explains available vaccines for the three respiratory viruses likely to be very active this fall and winter: COVID, influenza, and RSV. She also addresses other ways to protect oneself this winter.

For related links mentioned in this episode: https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/podcast/covid-and-fall-vaccines-2024-update/

You can also visit Dr. K's COVID page here:  https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/covid-and-vaccine-updates-for-aging/

text:
As a geriatrician, I’m often asked about atrial fibrillation (afib), a common heart rhythm issue in older adults. In this video, I sit down with Dr. Cara Pellegrini, a cardiologist and an expert in cardiac electrophysiology, to discuss what you need to know about afib, including its symptoms, diagnosis, and treatment options.

We cover everything from lifestyle changes and medications to devices like the Watchman, which helps reduce stroke risk. We also talk about the connection between afib and stroke, how blood thinners play a role, and special considerations for treating older adults, especially those who are frail or have dementia, like Alzheimer’s.

If you or someone you love is dealing with afib, this video offers practical insights on managing this condition in the elderly.

Get the related references and resources on the podcast show notes page here: https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/podcast/atrial-fibrillation-in-older-adults/

text:
Geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH, goes beyond Alzheimer’s disease to explain the most common types of dementia in older adults, and how doctors diagnose the specific type of dementia. She also covers mixed dementia and less common causes of dementia. Learn the most common early symptoms of Alzheimer’s dementia, vascular dementia, and Lewy body dementia, plus what we know about treating dementia in older adults. You’ll also learn about the newest (yet common) types of dementia pathology, such as LATE, hippocampal sclerosis, and cerebral amyloid angiopathy.

Geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH, explains the critical topic of unsafe driving in aging, shedding light on how aging impacts driving abilities and the key signs that indicate it might be time to stop driving. Dr. K also covers how to get someone to stop driving when it’s time to do so.
