subtitles.plaintext:
Is it normal for an aging parent to often forget things
that happened recently?
Or to keep asking the same question over and over again,
yet still be able to recall things that happened a long
time ago?
Stay tuned to find out.
Hello everyone.
Welcome to Helping Older Parents with Memory Loss,
a video podcast series that gives you strategies and information about
assisting aging parents who are experiencing memory or thinking problems.
I'm your host,
Dr. Leslie Kernisan board certified geriatrician and the founder of Better
Health While Aging,
and also of the Helping Older Parents online programs.
In today's episode,
I want to talk about something that I think is really
important to understand if you have an aging parent,
which is this: Is it normal to have short term memory
loss, as one gets older?
Now you may not have actually wondered if this is normal
or not.
In my experience,
many people believe that it is normal to develop short term
memory loss,
especially as people get into their eighties and nineties,
but here's the thing it's actually not normal to become very
forgetful as you get older.
Specifically, it is not normal aging if you've noticed your parent
is doing things like asking the same question repeatedly,
forgetting what happened recently,
like earlier in the day or earlier in the week,
or repeating the same stories or statements.
Now you may be thinking that well,
don't mental abilities decline somewhat as people get older.
Well, that is true.
That's because the brain,
just like all the rest of the body,
does experience what we call normal aging.
Now, today,
I'm not going to go into the deep science of what
is aging and how it affects cells and organs.
It is a really interesting topic,
and there's also really interesting research being done on this topic
at this time.
For now,
I'll just say that the effect of normal aging is that
cells and organs work less efficiently as people get older.
This is why we develop wrinkles or take longer to recover
from injuries as we age.
And in the brain normal aging means that your brain does
get a little slower when it comes to executing most thinking
processes. So for memory,
this can mean that it takes longer to remember something or
to figure something out.
Other things that usually fall into normal memory changes as people
get older,
include occasionally forgetting where you left things you use regularly,
such as glasses or keys,
having trouble remembering names for a bit,
or occasionally forgetting an appointment or walking into a room and
forgetting why you entered or becoming easily distracted or having trouble
remembering what you just read or the details of a conversation.
Last but not least,
it is normal to have a little bit of trouble and
find yourself not quite able to retrieve information that you have
on the tip of your tongue.
These types of mental slowdowns,
again are common and they are considered normal,
but it should be considered normal if your parent is unable
to remember recent events and they should not be repeating themselves
or repeating questions because they can't remember what has happened.
So again,
developing short-term memory loss is not normal as people get older.
So if you have an aging parent and you think you
perhaps are noticing some memory loss,
what should you do?
Well, first and foremost,
don't treat it as normal.
Instead, you need to treat it as a sign that there
might be something amiss with your aging parents brain function.
Now, where do you go from there?
This really depends on a few things briefly.
They are,
what's been happening with your parent in terms of their behaviors
and abilities.
How aware is your parent of their memory loss and how
do they feel about it?
Has the memory loss been brought to their doctor's attention and
have they been adequately medically evaluated?
Can their memory loss problems be treated or improved?
And that by the way,
is going to depend on what's found to be the underlying
cause of the memory problems when they get medically evaluated.
Another consideration is,
does your parent seem to need some support and assistance now
to maintain their health,
wellbeing, safety,
and ability to maintain their independence?
So those are some of the things that you'll want to
consider and how exactly to assess those things and what actions
to take and how to talk to your parent about this,
these are also really important things for you to know.
So I'll be breaking those down in upcoming episodes of this
series. Or if you would like to have a handy written
guide that you can consult as you listen,
or if you need to put your head together with a
sibling, I wrote a book for people just like you,
that lays out step by step processes for what you should
do if your parent is showing signs of memory loss,
or is otherwise worrying you.
And I wrote this book because I get asked about this
topic a lot,
and it's more than I can write about in one of
our online articles,
but now I'm making the video series because I know that
not everybody finds the book or wants to buy a book.
So we'll be covering a lot of similar information in this
series. But if you want an easy reference,
this will probably be the easiest way to reference my suggestions
as you go through this series.
So again,
my geriatricians key takeaway for you today is that short-term memory
loss is not a normal part of aging.
So if your aging parent has become forgetful or is repeating
themselves or otherwise seems to have developed a poor short-term memory,
please know that this is probably a sign of something being
off in their brain function.
Fortunately, they have you in their life to notice and to
help make sure that steps are taken to investigate and to
maintain their health and wellbeing.
And I'll be covering more of those steps you can take
in the upcoming episodes.
And now if you have a parent with memory loss,
I'd love to hear from you in the comments below,
had you been assuming that their poor short-term memory was normal
and how have their memory problems been affecting your family's life?
Okay. That's going to be it for today.
So thank you for watching this.
Thank you for thinking about your aging parents and I'll see
you in an upcoming episode.

What causes memory loss in aging parents, or in old age? Geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD, explains the 10 most common causes she checks for, and why it’s not necessarily Alzheimer’s disease. #memory #memoryloss #alzheimer Read more: https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/cognitive-impairment-causes-and-how-to-evaluate/

Get easy access to the guidance, support, & information you need, to help your aging parent with memory loss: https://betterhealthwhileaging.mykajabi.com/free-memory-loss-safety-training

If your loved one has developed memory loss in old age, you may be wondering if it’s a sign of Alzheimer’s disease, or another dementia. 

But since there are many other medical problems that can cause memory or thinking problems in later life (memory loss in 70s, 80s or 90s), it’s essential to not assume it’s Alzheimer’s until a medical evaluation has checked for other causes.

In this video, Dr. Kernisan explains the common causes of memory loss that geriatricians often check for.

Dr. Kernisan’s book: When Your Aging Parent Needs Help: A Geriatrician's Step-by-Step Guide to Memory Loss, Resistance, Safety Worries, & More 
https://www.amazon.com/Aging-Parent-Needs-Step-Step/dp/173615320X 

Subscribe to the Channel: https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCFpxvukIqCAUA7YizI-q9Dw?sub_confirmation=1

Video Chapters:
00:00 Causes of memory loss in old age.
02:04 Ten memory loss causes.
01:14 Medication side-effects.
02:26 Abnormalities in one’s blood chemistry.  
02:51 Problems with hormones, such as thyroid hormones.
03:11 Deficiencies in vitamins and other key nutrients.
03:25 Delirium. 
This is a state of worse-than-usual mental function that can be brought on by just about any type of serious illness. Delirium is especially common in hospitalized older adults.
03:53 Psychiatric illness.
04:30 Substance abuse.
Intoxication or chronic overuse of certain substances often impairs brain function.
04:54 Damage to brain neurons, due to an injury.
05:57 Infections.
Certain chronic or acute infections can affect brain cells directly.
06:31 Neurodegenerative conditions which damage brain cells over time. 
07:20 What causing my parent's memory loss?
Could it be reversed?

subtitles.plaintext:
If an older person is getting forgetful,
does that mean they have something like Alzheimer's disease or another
form of dementia or does it mean they have mild cognitive
impairment? Stay tuned to find out.
Hello everyone.
Welcome to Helping Older Parents with Memory Loss,
a video podcast series that gives you strategies and information about
assisting aging parents who are experiencing memory or thinking problems.
I'm your host,
Dr. Leslie Kernisan board certified geriatrician and the founder of Better
Health While Aging,
and also of the Helping Older Parents online programs.
In today's episode,
I'm going to address a frequently asked question,
which is this what causes memory loss as people get older?
Now, in a previous episode,
I explained that contrary to what many people believe,
if an older person has developed difficulty remembering what happened recently,
or if they keep repeating questions or statements,
that is not normal,
age-related slowing of memory.
And so it should not be considered normal aging.
That said it is fairly common for people to develop memory
loss as they get older.
And that's because of underlying health problems and the health problems
that cause memory loss or otherwise impaired brain function become much
more common as people age.
So what are these causes?
People often wonder whether it might be Alzheimer's disease or another
form of dementia.
Honestly, that's always a possibility in that Alzheimer's disease is quite
common, and it's pretty common that memory loss is one of
the earliest symptoms that families notice.
But you should not assume that memory problems are due to
early Alzheimer's or dementia,
because there are many other potential causes of brain dysfunction in
aging adults.
And we don't want to assume somebody has Alzheimer's or dementia
without having first checked for those other causes.
So let me now tell you about 10 memory loss causes
that I routinely check for when I'm evaluating memory problems in
an older adult.
The first is medication side effects.
There are so many commonly used medications that can slow brain
function and can cause or worsen memory loss or other thinking
problems. A second cause is abnormalities in a person's blood chemistry.
For instance,
abnormal levels of blood sodium calcium or glucose can all affect
brain function,
kidney or liver problems also often affect blood chemistry.
It's also possible for these blood chemistry abnormalities to be caused
by certain commonly used medications,
such as blood pressure medications.
A third cause that I often consider is problems with hormones,
such as thyroid hormones.
Now it's also possible for imbalances and estrogen and other sex
hormones to affect cognitive function.
That said,
this is probably more of an issue for perimenopausal women than
it is for my own patients who are usually in their
eighties and older.
A fourth cause to consider is deficiencies in vitamins and other
key nutrients.
Brain function is especially known to be affected by low levels
of vitamin B12,
other B vitamins and folate.
A fifth cause to consider is delirium.
This is a state of worse than usual mental function that
can be brought on by just about any type of serious
illness. And delirium is especially common in hospitalized,
older adults or in people who have had surgery,
but it can also occur due to an infection or due
to other health problems in older adults who are not hospitalized.
So that's an important cause to consider as well.
Number six that I want to tell you about is psychiatric
illness. Most psychiatric conditions in fact can cause problems with memory,
thinking or concentration,
especially in aging adults.
Psychiatric illnesses can also cause paranoia and other forms of late
life psychosis.
Now in older adults,
depression and anxiety are probably the most common psychiatric conditions we
encounter, but it's also possible for older adults to have bipolar
disorder, schizophrenia or other forms of major mental illness.
Usually these will have been diagnosed earlier in the older person's
life. Number seven that I want to tell you about is
substance abuse and or substance withdrawal.
That's because either acute intoxication,
so being currently using the substance,
or chronic overuse of certain substances,
such as alcohol illicit drugs,
or even prescription drugs,
that can often impair brain function.
So it's important to check for that as well.
Now, number eight is really a big one and that is
damage to brain neurons due to an injury.
And probably the most common form of damage is vascular damage,
which means damage caused by injuries and diseases affecting the blood
vessels. Most people have heard of major strokes and know how
they can affect the brain,
but what's by far more common is for the aging brain
to be affected by something.
We call cerebral small vessel disease,
which basically means injuries or diseases related to the very small
blood vessels in the brain.
Over years,
these accumulate in almost every older person and in some older
adults, they can accumulate to the degree that they actually start
to cause problems with brain function.
This is sometimes called vascular cognitive impairment and can potentially lead
to vascular dementia.
Another type of injury to consider are head injuries,
which can also be associated with temporary or longer lasting cognitive
impairment. But I would say that vascular injuries are much more
common. Number nine on my list is infections.
And this is not as common in older adults.
I would say,
as the causes above,
but certain chronic or acute infections,
either viral or bacterial,
can affect brain cells directly.
Now you might be thinking,
hold on a moment,
I've heard that urinary tract infections or other infections can potentially
cause memory loss or confusion.
Now that's true,
but I would say that's more due to delirium and it's
less about that infection directly affecting the brain cells.
And now for number 10 last but not least is neurodegenerative
conditions, which damage brain cells over time.
These include Alzheimer's disease,
Lewy body disease,
Parkinson's, and frontotemporal dementia.
And because these conditions slowly damaged brain cells over time,
usually years or even decades,
they often progress very slowly and can start by causing mild
cognitive impairment,
which then progresses to dementia.
And when we say it's progressive dementia,
that means that the memory loss or thinking problems have gotten
bad enough to affect independence in daily life tasks.
If it hasn't gotten bad enough to affect independence in daily
life tasks,
but there's definitely some memory loss or other cognitive problems,
we would call that mild cognitive impairment.
So those are the 10 causes that I think about for
memory loss in an older person.
Now, if you've been worrying about your aging parents or another
older relative,
you're probably thinking,
okay, but what's causing my parents' memory loss and could it
be reversed?
Those are great questions.
And I want to encourage you to keep thinking about them,
to answer those questions,
your parent is going to need to get medically evaluated.
If you want to know more about what that medical evaluation
should cover.
I have another video that covers this topic in depth.
Or you can also find this information in my book,
which includes a handy downloadable cheat sheet related to evaluation.
You may also be wondering how to actually get your parent
to the doctor or how to find out what type of
evaluation has been going on.
This can be tough because if your parent's been having memory
loss, they might not remember,
or even more common,
they might be reluctant to tell you.
But don't worry,
that's what I'll be covering in upcoming episodes,
so be sure to subscribe or otherwise stay tuned.
And I'll be seeing you again soon.

subtitles.plaintext:
When an aging parent develops memory loss or other signs that
might be early Alzheimer's disease,
how does that affect their ability to manage their self care
tasks, such as activities of daily living and instrumental activities of
daily living?
Stay tuned to find out.
Hello everyone,
welcome to Helping Older Parents with Memory Loss,
a video podcast series that gives you strategies and information about
assisting aging parents who are experiencing memory or thinking problems.
I'm your host,
Dr. Leslie Kernisan,
board certified geriatrician and the founder of Better Health While Aging,
and also of the Helping Older Parents online programs.
In this episode,
I'm going to talk more about something that is really relevant
if you're trying to figure out whether your aging parent needs
more help or can keep living at home,
which is this: how does memory loss usually affect an older
person's ability to manage their activities of daily living (ADL's) and
instrumental activities of daily living (IADL's)?
Now in the previous episode,
I explained what are ADL's and IADL's and why they are
so useful and important to assess when it comes to aging
adults. So if you haven't seen that video,
check it out.
I'll post the link below,
but briefly ADL's are the basic self care skills we learn
in early childhood,
walking, feeding yourself,
dressing yourself,
grooming toileting,
and bathing.
And then IADL's are the more mentally advanced self-care skills.
We usually learn as teenagers,
such as managing finances,
grocery shopping,
and meal preparation,
driving, home maintenance,
medication management,
and so forth.
Now most normal,
healthy adults are able to manage all their ADL's and IADL's
independently, but as we age,
or if we get sick or injured,
or if we develop certain types of chronic conditions,
we can start to have difficulty completing certain types of activities
on our own.
In geriatrics,
we refer to this as functional impairments or functional decline,
and it's something we really pay attention to because when older
adults start to experience functional decline,
that threatens their independence and ability to participate in life.
So we want to spot functional declines,
figure out why they're happening and reverse them when we can.
And if they can't be completely reversed,
we want to at least find ways to help the older
person compensate.
So for instance,
if somebody can't drive well anymore,
we want to find other ways to help them get to
where they need to go and want to go.
Or if they're having trouble walking,
we might consider a mobility device.
In the rest of this video,
I'll cover the most common ways that I see ADL's and
IADL's affected by memory loss,
thinking problems or early Alzheimer's disease.
This way you'll know what to look out for when it
comes to your own aging parent with memory.
Now in a different previous episode,
I explained that the difference between mild cognitive impairment and being
diagnosed with a dementia,
such as Alzheimer's dementia,
partly hinges on whether or not the memory problems or thinking
problems are bad enough to interfere with independence in daily life
tasks, basically independence with ADL's or IADL's.
So these changes I'll be describing could reflect early Alzheimer's or
another form of dementia.
If you're noticing them in your parent.
However, if you are noticing these problems,
keep in mind that you can't diagnose somebody with Alzheimer's or
another type of dementia,
just because they're having these problems.
And that's because there are many things that can cause memory
or thinking problems in older adults,
that's something I covered in a different episode on common causes
of memory loss.
Now, when it comes to memory loss and other forms of
early dementia,
such as early Alzheimer's disease,
it's usually the IADL's that are affected first.
So we'll start there.
How do IADLs change in early Alzheimer's?
So, as I explained in more depth in the previous video
IADLs are skills.
We usually learn as teenagers,
and most of them require some combination of organization,
memory and execution.
This means that most of them can be affected by early
dementia. Here are the most common ways that I see people
with memory loss have trouble with their IADLs.
Let's start with finances.
Finances are often affected very early on.
Common early problems include things like unopened or unpaid bills,
trouble making change,
or uncharacteristic financial transactions such as spending larger amounts than usual.
Another idea that is often affected early on is driving and
transportation. Common problems I see here include getting lost while driving,
having difficulty at intersections,
having trouble with parking,
getting an increased number of traffic tickets or parking tickets,
and difficulty managing public transportation.
Let's now talk about shopping and meal preparation.
So common problems that occur in memory loss might include lack
of enough food or supplies in the house.
This might be because the person is forgetting to go to
the store or when they go,
they might not get everything that they actually need.
We also often notice difficulty organizing and motivating to prepare meals.
You might notice burning food or leaving the stove on,
or perhaps your parent is misusing other kitchen appliances.
We also sometimes notice that a person seems to be overspending
online or at the store.
Now how about house cleaning and home maintenance?
Common problems here include the kitchen or house appearing messier or
dirtier than usual,
especially if it's a change compared to the way things used
to be.
Families also sometimes find that the older person has started to
stash items in odd places.
Or if there's a yard,
you might notice that it's becoming increasingly unkempt.
Let's move on now to managing communication such as phone and
mail. Common problems you might notice would be unopened mail piling
up, or perhaps the older person having difficulty contacting the right
person for a given circumstance.
You might notice that they're having increased trouble with their mobile
phone or smartphone or computer,
or perhaps you're noticing that they're forgetting to charge their devices
last but not least.
I want to touch on managing medications.
Now this IADL definitely gets affected by memory loss that said,
we also know that many cognitively normal older adults struggle with
medications because they are often hard to take correctly,
especially when people are on multiple medications,
which many aging adults are.
So I think this is the idea where it can be
a little harder to tell if a person is having abnormal
levels of difficulty or not.
But obviously people with memory loss certainly struggle even more with
their medications.
Common problems include forgetting to refill prescriptions,
taking medications too often,
or too little becoming unable to tell others what their medications
are and how often they take them and having trouble with
as needed medications,
such as those prescribed to manage pain or other symptoms in
short, virtually any IADL can be affected by memory and thinking
problems. And most older parents with memory loss will be struggling
with at least a few of these.
Although sometimes families may not notice unless they visit and observe
closely how their parent is managing.
Let's now talk about ADL's.
So again,
the activities of daily living are skills we learn in early
childhood: such as walking,
or otherwise getting around the home or outside,
feeding, as in getting food from a plate into one's mouth,
dressing, as in selecting appropriate clothes for the weather and occasion
and putting them on correctly,
grooming, which means adequately managing your personal appearance,
such as your hair,
your makeup,
or shaving,
toileting, which means getting to and from the toilet using it
appropriately and cleaning oneself,
and then bathing,
which means washing one's face and body in the bath or
shower. Now,
when it comes to a condition such as Alzheimer's or other
forms of dementia,
ADL's do eventually get significantly affected by dementia,
but usually it's later than the IADLs.
So for instance,
a person with Alzheimer's disease will eventually lose the ability to
walk and talk,
but that's usually only after years of symptoms.
Now that's not to say that we don't see ADL difficulties
in early Alzheimer's because we do in particular,
when people become forgetful,
they often start neglecting their grooming,
or they might make unusual dressing choices.
There are also some people with early Alzheimer's who get visual,
spatial difficulties very early on,
which basically means that it makes it hard for them to
figure out how to orient their clothes,
like which way is forward or which way is inside out.
And they can have difficulty putting them on.
So that's a group where we might see dressing difficulties quite
early. Otherwise the thing about ADL's and later life is that
older adults can easily have impairments due to physical health changes
that are common,
even in people who aren't experiencing memory loss or thinking problems.
So for instance,
even though trouble with balance and walking and continents and bathing
are all common in older adults with memory problems and are
associated with early Alzheimer's disease.
These are problems that are also very common in older adults
who definitely do not have Alzheimer's or another form of cognitive
impairment. That said if your parent has memory loss,
I would absolutely recommend that you check to see how they
are doing with their ADL's chances are that early on they'll
need your help and support more on the IADL side of
things. But if they are having any issues with ADL's,
it's important to know about that too.
So in short,
if your parent has been having memory or thinking problems,
expect that to manifest by effecting IADLs in particular,
but since many older adults have ADL difficulties as well,
I suggest you check for those two.
Now, once you've identified where your parent is having trouble with
IADL's or ADL's you'll want to work on two things first.
You'll want to make sure that the underlying cause of the
problem has been identified.
This usually requires medical evaluation.
Next you'll want to think about arranging for some form of
support or assistance or supervision.
If it seems like it'll help your parents have the best
possible quality of life safety or wellbeing achieving these is doable,
but it often requires some research and persistence to make it
happen. If you'd like to learn more about how to do
this and how to get around the most common challenges when
it comes to helping a parent with IADLs or ADL's,
I do have a free online workshop for families dealing with
memory loss that covers this.
The workshop has a focus on talking about safety issues in
particular, but the method I teach in that workshop can be
used to help your parent with any type of IADL or
ADL issue that comes up in your family.
So I'll post the link to that workshop in the description
of this video.
Otherwise for more on how to help aging parent with memory
loss, please subscribe and stay tuned because I'll be covering more
on this subject very soon.
Take care and hope to see you soon in the next
video.

channelDescription:
If you're over 60 and want to stay sharp, active, and independent as you age, you’re in the right place. On this channel, geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH, breaks down complex health topics into clear, practical steps you can take based on the best of geriatrics and aging science.

From understanding medications and memory changes to improving nutrition and preventing falls, every video helps you age with clarity and confidence. To get weekly tips directly from Dr. K, sign up for her free newsletter below.

Supporting an aging parent or relative? Check out Dr. K’s companion channel, Helping Older Parents, where she shares videos specifically about caregiving and eldercare.

Disclaimer: All content is for educational purposes only and is not a substitute for personalized medical advice.

text:
Is it time to live with COVID or should older adults still be taking precautions? What about Omicron BA.2? How did vaccines hold up against Omicron and when will COVID be endemic? Geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH, explains this and more, in this update.
For related links and Dr. K's latest 2022 COVID updates: https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/co...

0:00 Intro
9:13 The data on vaccines & boosters during Omicron
18:33 The data on Denmark "letting it rip" (& the impact on older adults)
21:47 How to OurWorldInData.org to compare US COVID data to that of other countries
28:58 What to know about the Omicron sister variant BA.2
39:30 What it would mean for COVID to be “endemic”
47:07 Dr. K's ideal societal approach to living with COVID
52:31 What you can do stay safer from COVID
54:06 Wastewater & other ways to monitor COVID in your local area

Update 2/25/22: The CDC released updated guidance re COVID and assessing local COVID-19 community levels today. Dr. K has posted written comments regarding this here: https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/co...

Covid News Summer 2023:    • COVID 2023 News: Summer COVID Update for O...  

Disclaimer: The material on the Better Health While Aging Youtube channel, including any exchanges in the comments section, is for informational and educational purposes only. Any comments Dr. Kernisan may make regarding an individual’s story or comments should not be construed as establishing a physician-patient relationship between Dr. Kernisan and a caregiver, or care recipient. None of Dr. Kernisan’s website, social media, comments, or group information should be considered a substitute for individualized medical assessment, diagnosis, or treatment. Please see the full disclaimer for more information: https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/di...

Constipation is common in later life, but it’s not an inevitable part of aging. Geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH explains why constipation happens in older adults, the signs to watch for, and how to build a safe, step-by-step plan to get regular again. You’ll learn which medicines commonly cause or worsen constipation, when to ask for a medical evaluation, and how to prevent complications like hemorrhoids or fecal impaction.

We cover practical fixes you can start today: hydration, fiber done right, prunes, toilet stools, gentle movement, how to choose over-the-counter laxatives that actually work, and how to use “maintenance” vs “rescue” treatments. You’ll also learnabout enemas, when to avoid certain products, how to adjust for frailty, and how to track progress so relief lasts.

location: All Episodes: Dr Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH – Better Health While Aging
channelDescription:
If you're over 60 and want to stay sharp, active, and independent as you age, you’re in the right place. On this channel, geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH, breaks down complex health topics into clear, practical steps you can take based on the best of geriatrics and aging science.

From understanding medications and memory changes to improving nutrition and preventing falls, every video helps you age with clarity and confidence. To get weekly tips directly from Dr. K, sign up for her free newsletter below.

Supporting an aging parent or relative? Check out Dr. K’s companion channel, Helping Older Parents, where she shares videos specifically about caregiving and eldercare.

Disclaimer: All content is for educational purposes only and is not a substitute for personalized medical advice.

text:
Get practical advice on COVID boosters in older adults and more. Board-certified geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH, explains what the latest research shows regarding the efficacy of COVID vaccines in older adults, whether this changes over time, what to know about boosters, how to stay safer during the holidays, and more.

For Dr. K's latest updates on COVID and vaccination, see https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/co...

None of Dr. Kernisan’s website, social media, comments, or group information should be considered a substitute for individualized medical assessment, diagnosis, or treatment.

title: 10 Causes of Memory Loss in Aging
location: All Episodes: Dr Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH – Better Health While Aging
channelDescription:
If you're over 60 and want to stay sharp, active, and independent as you age, you’re in the right place. On this channel, geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH, breaks down complex health topics into clear, practical steps you can take based on the best of geriatrics and aging science.

From understanding medications and memory changes to improving nutrition and preventing falls, every video helps you age with clarity and confidence. To get weekly tips directly from Dr. K, sign up for her free newsletter below.

Supporting an aging parent or relative? Check out Dr. K’s companion channel, Helping Older Parents, where she shares videos specifically about caregiving and eldercare.

Disclaimer: All content is for educational purposes only and is not a substitute for personalized medical advice.

problems, I always want to ask about symptoms of depression or
anxiety and ask about their mental health history to see if
a mental health issue might be contributing to the symptoms we're
concerned about.
Number seven on my list is substance abuse and or withdrawal.
So by substances,
I mean things like alcohol,
drugs, or even prescription medications,
such as sedatives or painkillers.
These definitely affect the brain and the brain can definitely be
impaired and not able to function well if people are intoxicated
and currently under the influence.
Or their brains can also be affected by chronic overuse,
basically chronic damage due to the substance.
And that's something we see,
especially with people who are chronic alcoholics.
But also,
if a person is used to using alcohol every day or
their prescription medication every day,
and they're not able to use it,
they can experience withdrawal and withdrawal in of itself can cause
confusion, thinking problems and brain dysfunction.
So when I'm considering what might be causing memory loss or
thinking problems,
I always want to know,
does this older person use any substances regularly or is there
a possibility they could be withdrawing from something.
Next number eight,
number eight on my list is damage to brain cells due
to injury.
And the most common form of injury that I think about
is what we call vascular damage.
So vascular,
it refers to the blood vessels of the brain and just
as you have blood vessels throughout the body and a network
of blood vessels for the heart,
we also have a network of blood vessels for the brain
and the brain very much needs the oxygen that comes in
through the blood vessels.
So if there has been damaged to those blood vessels,
that damages brain cells,
and that can cause memory loss and thinking problems.
If it's been a major blood vessel that was damaged,
that would be a major stroke.
And often people have obvious symptoms at the time they are
having that stroke,
but it's also possible for the teeny tiny blood vessels in
the brain to experience damage for various reasons often for reasons
that are very similar to the reason why people develop heart
disease: high blood pressure,
high cholesterol,
sometimes diabetes,
lots of inflammation,
lots of stress,
smoking. And so when the small blood vessels in the brain
are affected in this way and get damaged,
the brain cells around them can be damaged.
And this is sometimes called cerebral small vessel disease.
And if enough of the brain is damaged in this way,
it can cause memory loss and thinking problems.
So that's one form of damage to the brain cells that
is due to injury that I think about.
The other would be head injuries,
which can cause temporary or long-term brain function impairment.
So when I'm considering whether this is an issue,
I consider the age of the person,
their past medical history,
and we might consider a scan of the brain to see
if we see signs of damage in that way too.
I also ask if there have been any head injuries.
Next number nine on my list would be damaged brain cells
due to neurodegenerative disease.
Now this is number nine,
but it is quite quite common for people as they get
older, if they're lucky to get old enough,
to start experiencing some neurodegenerative diseases.
So what are these conditions?
These are conditions that basically accumulate usually in the brain and
slowly damage and kill neurons over time,
usually over years.
So these are diseases that take 10,
20 years often to have to show symptoms,
and then for the symptoms to progress.
You've heard of the most common neurodegenerative diseases.
They are things like Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease.
There are also other ones like Lewy body disease and frontotemporal
degeneration. These conditions are often the underlying cause of conditions such
as mild cognitive impairment,
which means a person is having some memory or thinking problems,
but they are not bad enough to interfere with day-to-day function.
And then there's dementia,
which is an umbrella syndrome describing a condition where people's brains
have changed to the point that it's a permanent change and
they have lost independence in some daily life tasks,
and it's not due to a psychiatric condition or something reversible.
And Alzheimer's disease is the most common underlying cause of dementia.
So that would be another potential cause of memory loss and
thinking problems in an older person.
And then number 10 on my list is infections.
So this I would say is less common,
but does happen.
So basically certain acute,
which means they're happening right now,
or chronic,
which means they've been going on for weeks or months,
certain acute or chronic infections can affect brain cells directly.
And the cause might be viruses,
bacteria, parasites,
a fungus.
So we don't routinely in geriatrics evaluate people for these kinds
of brain infections,
unless they're showing other symptoms or unless they've suddenly become quite
ill. And honestly,
when memory loss or thinking problems,
come on very suddenly,
we usually have another way of thinking about things,
than if it's been going on for months or years and
slowly getting worse,
which is the situation I mostly have in mind right now.
Now you may have heard of people developing memory loss or
thinking problems because they're sick from an infection like a pneumonia
or a urinary tract infection.
This does happen.
But in that case,
we think of it more as an example of delirium rather
than a direct infection to the brain,
because that's usually what's going on.
So those are the 10 causes that I think about the
most when I'm considering memory loss or thinking problems in an
older adult.
Now I do want to acknowledge one more because it's not
something we think about,
it's not something we evaluate a lot in geriatrics,
but it has been brought to my attention.
And I think it's,
you know,
reasonable to have it on the list,
which would be toxins.
So by toxins,
I mean things like heavy metals,
air pollutants,
water, contaminants,
pesticides. These are another potential cause of problems with brain function
in aging,
but in geriatrics - and I would say kind of mainstream
medicine, and I personally aim to practice the best of geriatrics
and the best of mainstream medicine for older adults - we
don't routinely check for these toxins.
There's a lot of interesting research going on.
It's also not clear right now,
how you would remove them or treat them.
So it's not part of my routine evaluation,
but you may hear other people mention it.
And that is why.
So those were my top causes of memory and thinking problems
in older adults.
And as you saw,
there are many medical conditions that can affect brain function.
So if you notice problems with memory or thinking in an
older parent or another older loved one,
or even yourself,
it's really important to get a medical evaluation so that these
can be checked for.
So now let me take you through what I believe doctors
should check when an older person is brought in from memory
or thinking problems.
These recommendations are based on my practice and the practice of
most geriatricians and are basically in line with what the expert
guidelines recommend for evaluation of cognitive impairments in an older person.
Because basically what we want to do is check for those
common causes that we just talked about to help rule them
in or out.
So here's my list.
First, what the doctor should do is ask about and document
the older person's concerns about their memory and thinking.
Now this can be tricky in that many older people are
either unaware that they're having memory loss or thinking problems,
or they are denying it,
or they're defensive and get upset when it's brought up.
So it often requires the doctor to be tactful about asking
about it.
There are tactful ways to ask,
but it's very important to understand for the older person what's
their awareness of the problem and how do they see it?
What are they most interested in or concerned about?
It's also important to compare their perception of the problem with
the perception that is reported by other people,
other family members and with what the doctor observes.
So that's definitely an important element.
The next element that's important is for the health provider to
get or request information about any signs of memory loss or
thinking problems from other people,
other family members like the spouse or someone else who lives
with the older person or other what we call informants,
which are basically people who've had a chance to see the
older person in their usual circumstances and might be able to
provide information.
Now, I have found that often doctors don't get around to
doing this.
It might be because the older person came to the appointment
alone or didn't want anybody with them.
Or they're not sure how to go about doing it,
but it's really important for them to try to get this
information because an older person who is experiencing memory loss or
thinking problems is not a reliable reporter of what is going
on with them.
So it's really important to get that information.
Also, you should know that it is not a HIPAA violation
for doctors to try to get this information.
And it's not a HIPAA violation for them to receive this
information from you as family.
So if you take a look at my related article on
Better Health While Aging I'll have a link to my article
on HIPAA and family,
because many people in the public don't understand HIPAA and actually
many health providers don't have the details quite right on what
HIPAA allows them to do and doesn't allow them to do.
But basically,
you can always tell a doctor what you have observed because
you as a family member are not a covered entity required
to observe HIPAA rules.
The covered entities are basically healthcare professionals,
insurance companies,
those of us whose work is healthcare.
And then a doctor should not be disclosing all of the
older person's health information to other people without their permission.
But they certainly are allowed to ask as part of an
evaluation. If other people have noticed anything or have anything to
share or contribute,
that is not a HIPAA violation.
So this is an important thing.
And if it's,
if you are concerned about somebody who has memory loss or
thinking problems,
I want to let you know that you are allowed to
relay what you've observed to the health provider.
You just want to think about doing so diplomatically and ideally
the older person you're concerned about would be agreeable to you
doing so.
Okay. So number three on my list is that the doctors
should ask about any difficulties managing daily life tasks.
So in geriatrics,
we call this assessing function.
So how is the person functioning in their daily life?
And the two big buckets that we consider our activities of
daily living and instrumental activities of daily living.
So really briefly,
activities of daily living are the basic skills that we often
learned in early childhood: walking,
talking, getting dressed,
feeding yourself,
getting to and from the bathroom,
bathing. And instrumental activities of daily living are the higher level
skills that we learn as teenagers that are usually required to
live independently as an adult.
So that includes things like driving or managing transportation,
finances, grocery shopping,
meal, preparation,
home maintenance,
managing medications.
As you can imagine,
if a person is having difficulty with memory or thinking,
it is often the instrumental activities of daily living that are
affected first.
And so health providers should really ask,
they can both ask the older person,
have you been having any trouble with any of your usual
activities or are you getting any help from anyone with anything?
And of course they should ask a family member or an
informant because again,
the older person may not be a reliable reporter of what
they need help with.
Understanding how the person's daily life is affected is matters both
in terms of making a diagnosis,
or edging towards one diagnosis or another,
if it's a question of mild cognitive impairment versus dementia,
but also it signals what the older person might need help
with and support with or where there might be safety issues.
So I think it's very important.
Number four on my list would be that the health provider
should check for other signs of behavioral mood or thinking symptoms.
So this is often related to,
are there signs of mental health issues or are there certain
behaviors or signs that might point us towards one type of
cause of cognitive impairment or another?
So specifically they should try to find out either from the
older person or from family if the older person has been
experiencing things like hallucinations,
delusions, personality changes,
apathy, depressive symptoms,
anxiety symptoms,
getting lost,
visual spatial problems.
If you would like a longer list of signs and behaviors
that are often associated with memory loss and thinking problems,
I'm going to be recording soon,
a related video,
21 signs to look out for,
and I'll have a longer list right there that you can
go through.
So next on my list,
number five,
the health provider should ask about any new symptoms or changes
to physical health.
Again, we're kind of trying to piece it together with,
could these memory loss or thinking problems reflect another problem with
the body somewhere else.
It's especially useful to ask about neurological symptoms,
such as new problems with walking,
new problems with balance,
new problems speaking or new problems with coordination.
Number six,
the health provider should try to find out if there are
any concerns about substance use and consider the possibility of abuse
or withdrawal.
So again,
this means inquiring with the older person about their use of
alcohol drugs,
prescription medications,
and also probably checking with family or others.
Number seven on my list,
very important I would say,
is to review all medications and focus on those that affect
brain function.
So especially the sedatives and tranquilizers and those anticholinergics,
those over-the-counter anti-histamines or sedating medications that interfere with brain function
and also looking out for the other anticholinergics that are often
prescribed for overactive bladder or for other causes.
Again, I have a list of seven types of commonly used
anticholinergics, which is one of the links in the article related
to this video,
if you want to know more about those.
And lest you think this is not important,
I can think of many patients where when we identify those
medications, that affect memory,
and we reduce them,
the person's memory and thinking really did get better.
So I think it's something very important and totally doable in
primary care.
Number eight is that the health provider should perform a physical
examination and what exactly they examine is going to depend,
you know,
on all the details they found out so far,
but generally you want to include a basic neurological evaluation,
especially of the nerves related to the face and head and
neck, because those are all nerves are related to brain function,
and those have particular importance in evaluating memory loss and thinking
problems. And the provider should also ask the older person to
stand up and watch how they walk,
have them walk across the room,
turn around and see.
It's also a good idea to check for what we call
Parkinsonism symptoms,
so they are associated with Parkinson's disease,
but can also be associated with related conditions such as Lewy
body dementia.
And for that,
it's checking for a tremor,
and in Parkinson's the tremor is at rest,
not when people are moving or trying to do something,
but when they're at rest,
when their hands are in their lap,
for instance,
so it's looking for a tremor there and then checking to
see if they feel stiff in the arms or other limbs.
Other things that would be looked for on the physical exam
are, again,
going to depend on the person's past medical history,
and onwhat else has turned up,
you know,
in the investigation.
Number nine for the evaluation is to specifically do some office-based
testing of the person's memory and thinking skills.
So I would call this assessing their orientation and then doing
a short office-based cognitive test.
So in medicine,
orientation means,
does the person know the date,
the day,
the month,
the year,
where they are and who they are.
And I look at notes and often the providers have not
specifically assessed this.
You really have to ask the older person,
you know,
I often say,
I'm going to ask you a few basic questions and they
might seem a little silly.
And then there's doing a few,
one of,
not a few; generally,
you just need to do one,
but there are a number of short office-based tests that can
be done to test memory and thinking.
So probably the shortest one that's well validated is called the
Mini-Cog. So that involves asking them to remember three items -
you tell them three items and later you ask them again
- and having them draw a clock and place the hands
at a certain spot.
So that doesn't take a lot of time.
And then there are other tests that can be done with
pen and paper.
They usually take 10 to 15 to 20 minutes.
The truth is they take longer when people are having memory
loss and thinking problems.
If you give them to somebody who's young and fine they
go quite quickly,
but those would be tests like the MOCA,
Montreal cognitive assessment,
the SLUMS,
St. Louis University Mental State Exam,
or even the mini,
excuse me,
the mini mental state exam.
That's an older test,
which is not considered a little less good.
So we don't use it very often in geriatrics,
but some providers are still using it.
And then number 10 on my list of what should be
done would be that the health provider should order laboratory testing
and consider brain imaging.
So I think it's a good idea to get blood tests
unless they've been done very recently.
And so what specifically is ordered is going to depend again
on the specifics of the situation,
but generally I'm checking a complete metabolic panel,
which would include blood electrolytes,
liver function,
kidney function,
checking, vitamin B12 levels,
checking thyroid tests,
and then potentially there could be additional tests like a complete
blood cell count,
if there's concern for an infection or another type of illness
that would be relevant to that test.
It's also fairly common for people to order a brain cat
scan or brain MRI.
MRI is better for showing the details of the brain when
it comes to memory loss and thinking problems.
But it does require sitting in the scanner for a good
45 minutes,
which can be hard for some older people who are having
memory loss or thinking problems.
On the scan it can,
it can show a variety of things.
What it will often show are signs of some small blood
vessel damage to the brain that is extremely common in older
people. Most older people have it actually,
if you scan their brains and it has imperfect correlation with
actual symptoms.
So one of the things that I often tell people is
that you can't really definitively rule in or out any cause
of memory and loss of memory loss and thinking problems with
the brain scan alone.
You know,
it's a piece of the puzzle,
but it shouldn't be,
it shouldn't be the only thing done and then these other
things are not done.
That's really not adequate.
So those are the 10 things.
So really,
if you put it together,
we kind of need four things to happen during this medical
evaluation. One is we need the health providers to document the
patient and family's concerns.
It should be in the chart that some concerns about memory
and thinking problems have been brought up and what they specifically
are, right?
So, you know,
either what the patient has noticed themselves that they're concerned about
or what the family has noticed in terms of memory loss
symptoms, or thinking problems.
Next, they really should document any difficulties that the older person
is having in their daily life tasks.
Again, because if the person is having a lot of difficulty,
we need to think about how can we provide more support
or assistance.
It might also make it more urgent to get other family
members involved.
Third, during these evaluations,
we want the health providers to do their own objective assessment
of the patient's memory and thinking abilities.
Even if it's something quite brief,
like just finding out if they know where they are,
the day and date,
who they are and whether they can do some,
you know,
fairly basic things like remember a few words and draw the
clock. And then lastly,
the health providers should really do that initial evaluation for a
common medical causes and contributors to worst brain function.
So especially the medication review,
possibly the basic labs,
and checking for a few of those other medical causes that
I mentioned.
Is this going to lead to a definitive diagnosis?
Not necessarily,
but it's an important starting point and it shouldn't be delayed.
So again,
if you're wondering,
how do you get this evaluation?
I want to tell you that you do not have to
wait for months to get seen at a special memory center
for this,
this, all,
this initial evaluation can be done in primary care.
And I would say should be starting in primary care.
Now it's extremely hard to do it in just one visit
unless the clinic is really prepared for these kinds of evaluations.
It is often going to take at least two visits,
but it is doable in primary care.
In short,
if you've gotten concerned about an older person's memory or thinking,
I hope you won't believe those two myths that,
you know,
it might be normal aging or that there's nothing to do.
Now you know what are the potential causes and now,
you know what should be done as part of a medical
evaluation. So I hope this will help you,
or your loved one,
get the evaluation that they need.
If you want more details,
be sure to check out my related article.
You can even print it out and use it as a
resource. And if you did find this video helpful,
please subscribe since I plan to continue to make videos related
to memory loss and other age-related health challenges.
So thank you so much.
Take care.
Thank you for watching and I'll see you,
hopefully in another video.

channelDescription:
If you're over 60 and want to stay sharp, active, and independent as you age, you’re in the right place. On this channel, geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH, breaks down complex health topics into clear, practical steps you can take based on the best of geriatrics and aging science.

From understanding medications and memory changes to improving nutrition and preventing falls, every video helps you age with clarity and confidence. To get weekly tips directly from Dr. K, sign up for her free newsletter below.

Supporting an aging parent or relative? Check out Dr. K’s companion channel, Helping Older Parents, where she shares videos specifically about caregiving and eldercare.

Disclaimer: All content is for educational purposes only and is not a substitute for personalized medical advice.

In this video, I’ll go into details regarding a type of medication that I wish all older adults knew about: anticholinergic drugs. #memory #brain #alzheimer #memoryloss #aging 

Get easy access to the guidance, support, & information you need, to help your aging parent with memory loss: https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/education-and-support/helping-older-parents-with-memory-loss/ 

Dr. K's related written article is here: 7 Common Brain-Slowing Anticholinergic Drugs Older Adults Should Use With Caution  https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/7-brain-toxic-drugs-seniors-should-avoid/ It’s essential to know which commonly used medications affect brain function and may worsen your memory. 

Learn why Benadryl, bladder relaxants, and a variety of other regularly prescribed anticholinergic drugs may impair brain function, exacerbate memory issues, and potentially raise your risk of Alzheimer's disease.

Board-certified geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH, explains what all older adults and their families should know about anticholinergic medications, including how to identify them and reduce them when possible.

This information is especially important if you've been worried about your memory, or if an older person might have mild cognitive impairment, or Alzheimer's disease, or another form of dementia.

Subscribe to the Channel: https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCFpxvukIqCAUA7YizI-q9Dw?sub_confirmation=1

Hello everyone.
I'm Dr.
Leslie Kernisan board certified geriatrician and the founder of Better HealthWhile
Aging dot net.
In this video,
I'm going to talk about one of the top things that
I address in my practice to help my older patients live
better, especially if there've been any concerns about memory loss or
brain health.
And that is what to know about a very common type
of medication that geriatricians consider risky for older adults.
They are called anticholinergics.
In geriatrics,
we always want to try to identify and then potentially cut
back on these medications,
because they slow brain function,
they can cause or worsen memory loss,
and they've even been linked to developing Alzheimer's or other forms
of dementia.
And this is not a fringe issue.
The impact of anticholinergics on brain function and aging brains have
been known about for decades.
Still these types of medications continue to be widely prescribed in
medicine, even to older people.
Also, many commonly used over the counter medications are anticholinergic,
such as Benadryl.
In fact,
when I review medications for older adults,
I find that many of them are regularly using an anticholinergic
medication. Sometimes even more than one.
Now you might be wondering how is it possible that so
many older adults are regularly taking medications that we know affect
brain function and might be bad for their brain health?
Well, this is happening really for two reasons.
On one hand,
most older adults have never heard of anticholinergics and have no
idea how common it is for them to be taking or
prescribed a medication that can affect brain function,
and that might cause or worsen memory loss.
And then on the other hand,
most practicing doctors have not been trained to avoid prescribing medications
that become riskier as people get older.
So even though in geriatrics,
we're trained to identify and reduce these medications,
most doctors have not had geriatrics training.
And so it's not top of mind for them.
And this is a known healthcare quality issue.
What's especially troubling is that in most cases,
there are more effective or safer ways to manage whatever symptom
or condition the anti-cholinergic medication has been prescribed for.
So basically,
we currently have a situation in which tens of millions of
older adults are unwittingly using medications that aren't good for their
brain, even though those medications aren't strictly necessary for their healthcare.
This has bothered me for a while.
And so I've concluded that to change the situation we need,
not only to change what doctors are doing and how they're
trained, but we also need to help more older adults and
families learn about this type of medication so that they can
play a role in spotting them,
in avoiding them,
and in partnering with their health providers to use them with
caution. So that is my goal for this video.
Specifically, I'm going to explain to you what makes a medication
anticholinergic so that you understand what it means,
and what it means for the body and brain,
and why these tend to affect people more as they get
older. And then I'm going to take you through seven commonly
used types of anticholinergic: what they are,
what they're usually prescribed for,
so that you'll know what to look out for.
Let's get started.
Now, what does it mean for a medication to be anti-cholinergic?
Well, an anticholinergic is a medication that has the chemical property
of blocking or otherwise diminishing the effects of a very important
neurotransmitter called acetylcholine.
A neurotransmitter is a compound that helps neurons,
so that means nerve cells,
communicate whether they are in your brain or elsewhere in the
body. And it turns out that acetylcholine is used quite a
lot by brain cells.
Your brain cells need to use acetylcholine to communicate with each
other in order to help you think,
remember, and use your brain for other cognitive functions.
Acetylcholine is also widely used outside the brain.
In fact,
it's used throughout the body often in ways related to what
we call the parasympathetic nervous system.
So basically the body has something called the autonomic nervous system,
which is not under your voluntary control,
but regulates a lot of your bodily functions.
And one part of it is the sympathetic nervous system,
which generates what people often call the "fight or flight" response.
That system mostly does not use acetylcholine.
However, the counter to that system,
the parasympathetic nervous system,
which generates a lot of your "rest and digest" functions in
the body,
that one does heavily rely on acetylcholine.
So anticholinergic drugs often have side effects related to the eyes,
the bowels,
the bladder,
or the mouth,
things like dry eyes,
dry mouth,
constipation. These side effects can definitely be problematic in older adults,
but honestly,
it's the brain side effects that usually I find the most
concerning because when acetylcholine is blocked in the brain,
this leads to decreased brain function,
which people often experience as sedation.
Now this may be why people are taking the drug.
Lots of people take Benadryl to help them sleep,
and this might be something that you've tried yourself.
And a little sedation might sound benign to you.
But when the brain is older or has otherwise become vulnerable,
that acetylcholine blocking can become more problematic.
It can cause or worsen memory loss.
In people who have already symptoms of Alzheimer's or another dementia,
it can make them worse.
And it also,
because it's making people drowsier and slower,
can increase fall risk.
In fact,
it turns out that anticholinergics literally have the opposite effect of
drugs that were developed to treat Alzheimer's and other dementias.
So you may have heard of a medication that is called
Aricept. The generic name is donepezil.
This was the first blockbuster medication for the treatment of Alzheimer's.
And what it does,
is it increases acetylcholine in the brain by blocking the brain
enzyme that breaks it down.
And this drug was developed because it was noticed that people
who were experiencing Alzheimer's and some other forms of dementia seem
to have not enough acetylcholine in the brain.
And so this drug was developed to help boost it.
So you can imagine that if we are giving drugs to
help boost acetylcholine in the brain of people with Alzheimer's,
maybe it's not great for the brain,
when we give people medications that have the usually unintended effect
of blocking some acetylcholine function in the brain.
And in fact,
research has shown that chronic use of anticholinergics is linked to
having a higher risk of developing Alzheimer's later in life.
So I hope you now see why geriatricians love to hate
anticholinergics. Let me now take you through seven types of very
commonly used anticholinergic medications,
so that you'll know what to look for.
And in this video,
I'm going to focus on medications that are especially used in
the outpatient setting.
All of these medications are on what we call the "Beers
List." That is a list maintained by geriatricians for the past
several years of medications that are potentially inappropriate for older adults,
because they're risky.
So they are medications that older adults should avoid or use
with caution.
And all the medications that I'm going to tell you about
in this video are on that list.
So first type of anticholinergic medication,
I want you to know about are sedating anti-histamines and these
are often available over the counter in drug stores,
pharmacies, and grocery stores.
The most common one is probably diphenhydramine.
The brand name is Benadryl.
Now you may also be wondering what about other anti-histamines that
are now available over the counter,
such as loratadine,
brand named Claritin.
So it turns out that the non-sedating antihistamines are much less
anticholinergic, so these are safer for aging brains.
And so if you're having allergy symptoms,
I would definitely recommend using a non-sedating anti-histamine rather than a
sedating one.
Next on my list of common anticholinergics you should know about
are the PM versions of over-the-counter pain killers.
So things like Tylenol PM,
NyQuil or Advil PM.
And this is because the PM in those medications comes from
mixing in a mild sedative,
usually a sedating anti-histamine with the analgesic.
So next time you're in the drug store,
if you pick up one of these items and take a
look at the ingredients,
you'll see that probably it includes either diphenhydramine,
so again,
that's brand named Benadryl,
or another sedating antihistamine called doxylamine.
Both of these are strongly anticholinergic.
And so I would recommend being careful about using these.
There are also available over-the-counter sleep aids,
such as Unisom.
Well, if you look at the ingredient,
it's generally just diphenhydramine or another form of sedating anti-histamine and
it is anticholinergic.
So if you want to manage pain at night,
I would just take the straight-up painkiller.
And if sleep is an issue,
then I would recommend talking to your doctor about another way
to manage your sleep,
that doesn't involve these types of medications.
And you should also be careful about other sedatives.
We'll cover that in another video.
Number three,
on my list of types of anticholinergics you should know about,
are medications for overactive bladder.
So that's because it's the parasympathetic nervous system that manages a
lot of bladder function.
And so when you block acetylcholine,
the bladder relaxes and doesn't squeeze as hard,
or as often.
These kinds of urinary issues are very common for older people,
so many older adults have been prescribed a bladder relaxant,
such as oxybutynin (brand name Ditropan),
tolterodine (brand name Detrol) or solifenacin (brand named Vesicare).
Unfortunately, all of these medications are quite anticholinergic.
So that doesn't mean that it's absolutely out of the question
to use them,
but it is something to keep in mind,
because often there are other ways to manage overactive bladder symptoms
or other urinary symptoms.
And it's important to ask your health provider about those before
you use this type of medication chronically,
or in a person who is having memory loss symptoms.
Number four,
on my list of anticholinergic medications,
are medications for vertigo,
motion sickness or nausea.
So one common example is meclizine,
the brand name is Antivert,
which is often used to treat benign positional vertigo.
So this is a condition that does affect older adults,
where people have a feeling of spinning around them,
or the floor tilting,
and it's related to a condition affecting their inner ears.
This has historically been treated with meclizine,
but it turns out that there are special forms of physical
therapy that can also treat vertigo.
You also want to make sure if an older person is
taking this medication that they truly do have vertigo.
I once had a patient who was very attached to this
medication because he often felt wobbly or dizzy.
But when I asked him about it,
he actually felt lightheaded when he stood up because his blood
pressure was coming down when he stood up,
that's also very common in older adults.
And that was not a problem that could be fixed with
the meclizine.
For that,
we had to adjust his blood pressure medications.
So we ended up adjusting his blood pressure medications and also
realizing he didn't need that meclizine.
And that was safer for him.
He was about 90.
Another medication that you've probably heard of that is used for
motion sickness or nausea would be dimenhydrinate,
brand named Dramamine.
So this too is quite anticholinergic.
So if you only use it every once in a great
while, that's okay.
But again,
something to keep in mind,
if you're reaching for it often.
The fifth type of anticholinergic medication you should look out for
are medications prescribed for itching.
So again,
these are usually some form of strong oral anti-histamine such as
again, diphenhydramine,
Benadryl, or there's another one hydroxizine,
the brand name is Visteril.
If you have been experiencing itching,
then it would be useful to talk to your health provider
about whether there might be a topical cream that could be
used, that often has fewer side effects for older people,
or is there another way to manage this problem?
Actually, a lot of older people end up quite itchy because
they have dry skin and just really doubling down on moisturizers
and skin care can improve their itching.
Number six,
on my list of commonly used anticholinergics are medications for nerve
pain. Specifically,
there's an older class of antidepressants that we call tricyclic antidepressants,
which now have kind of fallen out of favor for treating
depression, because we have a whole crop of newer anti-depression drugs,
specifically the SSRI selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors,
that we use for depression.
But that older class of tricyclics used to also be used
to treat nerve pain.
And so sometimes they're still prescribed for nerve pain.
Even though,
again, we now have some newer better medications for nerve pain.
So some examples of this type of medication are amitriptyline,
the brand name is Elavil,
and nortriptyline,
the brand name is Pamelor.
These medications are also sometimes prescribed to treat shingles because a
while back,
we thought that using these medications might reduce the risk of
developing the post shingles nerve pain,
it's called post-herpetic neuralgia.
But actually now the research indicates that maybe these tricyclic antidepressants
are not particularly effective for preventing that.
So probably what's best if you don't want to get pain
from shingles is to get the shingles vaccine.
And otherwise,
if you find that you are taking one of these tricyclic
antidepressants, I would recommend bringing it up with your health provider
to see if there might be an alternative way to manage
whatever the tricyclic was prescribed for.
And then number seven on my list of commonly used anticholinergics
are muscle relaxants.
So these are often prescribed for back or neck pain.
And probably the most common example would be cyclobenzaprine.
The brand name is Flexeril.
So it's important to know that cyclobenzaprine is quite anticholinergic.
So especially for older adults,
we want to be careful about using it often or regularly.
Also, back pain and neck pain are other conditions that often
can be managed through other methods.
And it's not clear from the research that using cyclobenzaprine particularly
improves outcomes beyond the other ways that we manage back pain.
So those are the seven really common types of medication that
are anticholinergic.
Now I'm going to add one more,
it's off on its own because this particular medication is anticholinergic,
but the other medications in the same group are not.
And that medication is paroxetine,
the brand name is Paxil.
So this is a medication that is in the class of
again, SSRI antidepressants,
so selective serotonin re-uptake inhibitors,
and they are used both for depression and for anxiety.
So most of the medications in this class are not anticholinergic,
but Paxil is,
and that's why in geriatrics,
we almost never prescribe this for depression or anxiety.
And as people get older,
if they come into our practice,
we often try to transition them to one of the other
SSRIs that we consider safer for older people,
such as escitalopram,
citalopram, or sertraline,
the brand names are Lexapro,
Celexa and Zoloft.
So that covers my list of commonly used anticholinergic medications.
I have focused mostly on medications that are used in the
outpatient setting.
There are many more medications that we use less often,
or that we use,
especially in the hospital that are anticholinergic as well,
such as certain nausea medications,
and certain medications for other more specialized conditions.
If you want to see a longer list of anticholinergic medications,
in the description for this video,
I'll have a link to my related Better Health While Aging
article. And in that article,
we have a link to a longer list that is available
online. Now,
who should avoid anticholinergics?
So, as you can see,
these medications are pretty common.
They're everywhere.
Do we all need to be avoiding them?
Well, I think there are three groups in particular who should
make a special effort to identify and avoid anticholinergics if possible.
So first,
people who are concerned about their memory or thinking right now.
So if you've noticed some symptoms of memory loss or thinking
problems, or you've gotten worried about your brain function,
I would definitely recommend making an effort to minimize use of
anticholinergics. Two would be people who have actually been diagnosed with
a cognitive condition,
such as mild cognitive impairment or a dementia such as Alzheimer's
disease. So most of those people have an underlying change to
their brain.
Their brain is damaged and vulnerable.
Their brain cells,
right, are changing.
That's the nature of Alzheimer's disease is that it's slowly changing
and diminishing the function of your brain cells.
So those people especially need all the help they can get
for their brain cells to work at their best.
And we want to be careful about anticholinergics in that group
of people.
And then third would be people who particularly want to minimize
their risk of developing Alzheimer's or another kind of condition later
in life.
Now, if you're worried about the long-term risk associated with anticholinergics,
you should know that as best we can tell,
the risk seems to be associated with cumulative use: both how
long and how high the doses.
So if you've only used anticholinergic medications occasionally here or there,
I wouldn't be too concerned.
If you've used it regularly for a while,
that's not ideal,
but you know,
the past is past; just think about what could you maybe
change or do right now to reduce your use of those
medications. And so what should you do if you actually have
been taking an anticholinergic?
So again,
if it's just occasional,
I wouldn't worry about it,
but otherwise,
in general,
the principle with risky medications is that we want to look
at them and think about,
can we stop if at all possible,
or can we switch to a safer option?
Or if not,
how can we reduce it to the lowest effective dose?
So if the anticholinergics that you've been taking are over-the-counter,
generally, you can just stop those on your own.
But if they have been prescribed,
I do not recommend that you stop or reduce on your
own. Instead,
I would highly recommend that you bring it up to your
usual healthcare provider,
your doctor,
or you could potentially talk to a pharmacist,
and that you ask them to explore alternatives and ways that
you might reduce your use of this medication.
It can help to do your research first.
So specifically I recommend thinking about what symptom or problem was
this anticholinergic medication prescribed for.
And then you could do a little research online to find
out what are other ways to manage this condition.
So for instance,
there are often non-drug ways or ways that don't require anticholinergics
to manage urinary symptoms or pain or allergies.
So having done that research before you come in to the
health provider,
it can help ensure that you'll consider all the options and
all the safer options,
when you talk with your health providers.
Now, in some cases,
there actually are not any good,
easy options for managing a certain symptom or condition without an
anticholinergic. If that is your situation,
and it seems like you're going to have to continue regularly
using an anticholinergic,
please don't panic or worry about it too much.
In general,
it is reasonable to continue taking a risky medication,
if the likely benefits outweigh the risks,
and if alternatives have been explored and found wanting.
Furthermore, there are other ways that you can maintain your cognitive
health or help your brain think the best it can be.
So yes,
in a perfect world,
maybe you wouldn't be taking the anticholinergics,
but if you do need to,
don't worry about it,
just look for other ways to maintain your best possible health.
So now you know about the seven common types of anticholinergic
medication that you can look out for and try to minimize
if possible.
Now there are other types of medication that I would also
recommend avoiding if you're worried about memory and I will be
making more videos about those soon.
In the meantime,
for more videos about aging health topics,
including videos about helping aging parents,
please subscribe to the channel or come visit us at Better
Health While Aging dot net.
Take care.
Thank you for watching and hope to see you again.

channelDescription:
If you're over 60 and want to stay sharp, active, and independent as you age, you’re in the right place. On this channel, geriatrician Leslie Kernisan, MD MPH, breaks down complex health topics into clear, practical steps you can take based on the best of geriatrics and aging science.

From understanding medications and memory changes to improving nutrition and preventing falls, every video helps you age with clarity and confidence. To get weekly tips directly from Dr. K, sign up for her free newsletter below.

Supporting an aging parent or relative? Check out Dr. K’s companion channel, Helping Older Parents, where she shares videos specifically about caregiving and eldercare.

Disclaimer: All content is for educational purposes only and is not a substitute for personalized medical advice.

Have you noticed worrisome changes in your aging parent? Wondering if they can still live on their own? Check out Dr. Kernisan's book on this topic, which includes cheatsheets and checklists: https://www.amazon.com/dp/B08QTXTWXW #elderly #aging #brain #memoryloss
